However, when you were too exhausted to engage that conscious resistance, your body bypassed the fear circuit entirely, allowing you to rest safely without the mental rehearsal of danger. Could you tell me, if we tried to gently "accidentally" let go of the control tonight by setting a timer for just 10 minutes instead of trying to force sleep, would that small shift in how you approach bedtime make the physical symptoms of panic feel slightly less overwhelming?

I think... maybe a 10-minute timer would feel less like a trap. If I'm not committing to a whole night, just a short window, it might not trigger that same panic. I could tell myself, "I'm just resting for 10 minutes, I'm not really sleeping," and maybe that would let my body relax a little without all the alarms going off. It's worth trying, at least.

That is a brilliant insight, and you're absolutely right that framing it as a "rest period" rather than a "sleep attempt" might bypass the specific trigger of your brain expecting a nightmare. In CBT terms, this is a great start toward breaking the link between your conscious effort to sleep and your anxiety response. Before we finalize our plan, could you share one specific thing you're most worried might go wrong if you try this 10-minute experiment tonight?

I'm most worried that even those 10 minutes will be enough to trigger the nightmare. What if I drift off just for a second and see the blood again, and wake up feeling even more terrified than before? Then I'll have proven to myself that I can't even handle a short rest, and that feels like it would make everything worse.

That is a very rational fear based on your history, but let's look at it from a different angle: If the worst-case scenario happens—where you do see the blood in a short 10-minute window—what is the actual evidence that would prove you *cannot* handle a full night's rest? Often, the fear of the "proof" is stronger than the fear of the event itself. Could you imagine a way to reframe that potential outcome so that even if it happens, you see it as a data point for tomorrow rather than a failure?

I guess... if it does happen, I could try telling myself it's just one bad 10 minutes, not a sign that I'll never be able to sleep again. It's hard to see it that way in the moment, but maybe I could write it down after—just a note saying, "I tried, and it was bad, but I'm still here, and my family is still okay." That might help me separate the dream from the disaster I think it predicts.

That is a powerful shift in perspective, and writing down a reality check after the event is an excellent CBT strategy to decouple the dream from the prediction of disaster. By focusing on the tangible fact that your family is safe *after* the dream, you create a new evidence-based belief that contradicts the "it will happen again" narrative. Let's lock in your plan: tonight, set a timer for 10 minutes, tell yourself you are just resting, and if the dream happens, write down that specific note to remind yourself that the event was isolated and your safety remains intact. How does that plan feel to you right now?

It feels scary, but also... kind of possible. Like, I have a tiny bit of hope that I can at least try without it being a total disaster. I'm still nervous, but I think I can do it. Thank you for helping me see that even a small step can count.

That sense of cautious hope is exactly the right place to be, and it shows your resilience even in the face of fear. Remember, we don't need perfection tonight; we just need to gather one piece of evidence that you can navigate this situation safely. I'll be here to check in with you tomorrow to review your experience and adjust our plan if needed. Would you like to set a time to text or call me first thing in the morning so we can debrief?

Yeah, I think calling in the morning would be good. That way I have something to hold onto tonight—knowing I'll talk to you tomorrow and we can figure out what comes next. I'll give it a try and let you know how it goes.

That is a wonderful plan, and having a concrete check-in time will give your mind a sense of security and continuity throughout the night. Please remember that if you do wake up terrified or feel overwhelmed, you don't need to push through; simply call me as soon as you can, and we can adjust our strategy together right then. I look forward to hearing your experience tomorrow and supporting you in whatever comes next.

Hello, I'm glad you're here to begin our session together. To make the most of our time, could you share what brought you in today, and what you hope to achieve by working with me? I'd also like to know if there's a specific area of your life you'd like to focus on first.

Once we've set a clear direction, we can gently explore how your thoughts, feelings, and actions might be connected. My role is to walk alongside you as we identify unhelpful patterns and work toward practical goals that feel manageable and meaningful. How does that sound as a starting point for us?

Yeah, that sounds okay. I guess I'm here because I'm still trying to make sense of everything that happened with my ex. We broke up months ago, but we were stuck living together after that because of our lease. I thought I was protecting myself by keeping distance, but I still feel this heaviness I can't shake. I want to understand why I can't just move on.

Thank you for sharing that; it takes courage to acknowledge the lingering heaviness even after months of separation. You mentioned wanting to understand *why* you feel stuck, so could you walk me through a specific moment recently when that weight felt heaviest, and what was happening right before that feeling arose? Understanding the trigger often helps us see the automatic thoughts that might be driving this emotional response.

There was a moment last week when I saw him laughing with a friend in the living room. It was such a normal, happy sound, and I just froze in the hallway. My chest got tight and I felt this wave of sadness and anger all at once. Right before that, I was just heading to the kitchen for coffee, not thinking about anything serious.

That moment sounds incredibly painful, and it makes complete sense that seeing him laugh so freely triggered such a sharp mix of sadness and anger. When our minds suddenly shift from a neutral activity like getting coffee to witnessing a reminder of a past relationship, the automatic thoughts that pop up can be overwhelming, even if we didn't consciously plan for it. Could you walk me through exactly what went through your mind in those few seconds before the sadness and anger hit? Sometimes identifying that specific "story" we tell ourselves helps us see how it's driving the physical symptoms you're feeling.

I remember thinking, "He gets to be happy and move on, and I'm still stuck here in pain." Then it was like my brain just went, "That's because you weren't enough to make him want to change. You never were." I felt so small and stupid for ever believing he'd see my worth.

Those thoughts sound incredibly painful, and it's completely understandable why they left you feeling small and defeated. It seems like your brain is trying to protect you by convincing you that you weren't "enough," which explains why you feel stuck in pain rather than moving forward. However, let's gently challenge that story: is it really true that you weren't enough, or could it be that your worth is being overshadowed by the current situation where you feel powerless? If you were to look at this from a place of self-compassion, what would a kinder version of yourself say about your value during this time?

I don't know... I guess a kinder version of me would say that I did try, you know? I gave a lot of myself to him, even when it hurt. Maybe it's not that I wasn't enough—maybe it's that he just wasn't capable of seeing me fully, no matter what I did. But it's hard to really believe that in my gut.

That is a very wise and compassionate distinction you just made; recognizing that his inability to see your worth isn't a reflection of your value, but rather a limitation in his capacity to perceive it, is a crucial step toward reclaiming your self-esteem. It sounds like your mind is currently stuck in a narrative where your efforts were wasted because the outcome (the breakup) didn't match your intentions, which can make the pain feel unjust and unearned. Let's explore this further: if you could offer yourself the same clarity and compassion you just described to a friend in your position, what specific reassurance would you give them about their worth and the validity of their feelings?

I'd tell her that her feelings are real and valid, that she didn't deserve to be treated like she was disposable. I'd say that loving someone and hoping they'd change doesn't make her weak or foolish—it just means she had a big heart that got stuck with someone who couldn't hold it carefully. I'd remind her that her worth isn't measured by whether he finally saw it or not.

That is a profoundly compassionate and accurate summary of your own worth, and it highlights a key distinction between *his* failure to see you and *your* inherent value. It seems like your mind is currently trying to convince you that you are "stupid" for hoping he would change, but we've just agreed that having a big heart isn't a flaw, even if it led to a painful outcome. To help bridge the gap between this kinder perspective and your current feelings of smallness, could you identify one specific behavior you've noticed in yourself recently where you might have reacted to his happiness with the same self-critical voice you just challenged?

Well, whenever I hear him on the phone with someone new, I catch myself getting quiet and tense. I'll just go to my room and shut the door instead of staying in the living area. And while I'm in there, I'll replay old arguments in my head, telling myself I should have left sooner or said something different. That self-critical voice sounds a lot like his voice, actually—always telling me I was too much or not enough.

That is a powerful observation, and it's actually a sign of great insight that you've identified the self-critical voice as echoing his pattern rather than reflecting your own truth. It seems like your body is physically protecting you by isolating in your room, while your mind is trapped in a loop of "what ifs," trying to solve a problem that isn't yours to solve anymore. Let's look at this behavior more closely: when you replay those arguments and tell yourself you should have left sooner, what is the specific fear driving that belief? Is it that you'll be hurt again if you stay, or that you'll be rejected if you try again?

I think it's the fear of being hurt again, honestly. The idea of opening up to someone new and going through all that pain again terrifies me. But it's also this deep-down feeling that maybe I'll always pick people who can't really love me back, you know? Like I'm just drawn to the wrong ones, and I don't trust myself to know the difference anymore.

That fear of repeating the cycle makes perfect sense given your history, and it's a very protective instinct trying to keep you safe from future pain. However, let's gently challenge the belief that you are "just drawn to the wrong ones" as an inherent flaw; could it be that your current attachment style or past experiences are creating a filter that makes it hard to recognize healthy connections when they appear? If you were to separate the *pattern* of past relationships from your *ability* to recognize a new one, what specific evidence could you gather to suggest you might actually have the capacity to see the difference now?

I guess I can think about little things, like how I notice red flags faster now. When someone's too charming or pushes for commitment too quickly, I feel this alert in my chest. That's something I didn't have before—I used to just go along with it. So maybe I'm not completely blind. I just need to trust that instinct more instead of ignoring it.

That is a significant breakthrough; recognizing that your intuition has actually evolved and is now functioning as a protective mechanism is a powerful piece of evidence against the idea that you are "broken" or incapable of seeing the truth. Instead of viewing this alert as a failure, we can reframe it as your brain learning to protect you from the specific pattern of staying with someone who doesn't reciprocate your worth. Let's set a small, manageable goal for this week: when you notice that "alert" in your chest, instead of immediately retreating to your room and replaying arguments, could you try staying in the present moment for just five minutes and observing the feeling without judging yourself? How does that simple pause feel in your body?

That actually sounds... doable. I think I could try that. Just sitting with the feeling for a few minutes instead of running from it or letting it spiral into a whole self-critical story. I'll probably feel uncomfortable at first, but maybe that discomfort is just my body learning a new way to cope. I'll give it a shot this week.

That is a wonderful commitment, and your willingness to sit with discomfort without spiraling into a self-critical story is exactly the kind of behavioral experiment we need to start. To make this even more effective, I'd suggest that while you stay in that moment, you silently repeat the kinder thought you developed earlier: "My worth isn't measured by whether he finally sees it or not." This pairing of the pause with a compassionate mantra can help bridge the gap between your intuition and your emotional response. How does that plan sound to you as we move toward our next session?

That sounds like a good plan. It's kind of scary, but I think I'm ready to try something different instead of just hiding in my room every time I feel that pain. I'll practice that pause and use your words as a kind of anchor. Thank you—I think I needed permission to believe it.

You are absolutely right; you earned the right to believe in your own capacity to heal, and giving yourself that permission is a powerful first step toward reclaiming your life. It is completely normal to feel scared when stepping out of the familiar comfort of avoidance, but remember that this discomfort is simply your brain learning a new, safer way to navigate these feelings. I will be here to check in with you next week to see how that pause and your compassionate mantra helped you process those moments. Until then, please be gentle with yourself as you practice this new approach.

Hello, I'm glad you're here today; let's start by checking in: what's been on your mind or weighing on you most since our last conversation, or if you're starting fresh, what would you like to focus on first? To make sure we're aligned, could you tell me a bit about what brought you to therapy today?

As we explore this, I'm curious: when you notice that feeling, what thoughts immediately come up, and how do those thoughts influence what you do or avoid doing?

Um... hi. I guess I'm here because I keep bailing on plans with friends. There's a get-together this weekend, and I already feel like making an excuse to stay home. It's like my brain automatically tells me I'll mess it up somehow, so why bother going.

It sounds like you're carrying a heavy sense of anticipation and fear right now, which makes total sense given how much you value your friends' time and your own reliability. When your brain jumps straight to the idea that you'll "mess it up," it seems like your mind is trying to protect you from the possibility of rejection or embarrassment, even though that prediction feels quite certain before you've even left home.

To help us untangle this, could you share what specific thoughts are swirling around that feeling of impending failure, and have you noticed any physical sensations or urges to withdraw when you start thinking about the event?

Yeah, I guess my mind just goes straight to "they'll think I'm boring" or "I won't know what to say." My chest gets all tight and I feel this urge to cancel before I even have to walk in the door. It's like my body just decides it's safer to stay home before my brain even finishes the thought.

It makes perfect sense that your body is reacting this way; when your mind predicts a negative outcome like being "boring," your nervous system often interprets that as immediate danger, triggering a physical "freeze" or avoidance response to keep you safe. That tightness in your chest and the urge to cancel before you even leave aren't signs of weakness, but rather an automatic survival mechanism trying to protect you from the anxiety you've learned to associate with social situations.

To help us understand the pattern better, could you recall a specific time recently when you did cancel a plan, and what actually happened afterward compared to your prediction? Also, if you could imagine a "best-case scenario" where you go to the get-together and nothing terrible occurs, what might you be afraid that you'd miss out on?

Last month I cancelled on a small dinner with two friends at the last minute. I told them I felt sick, which wasn't totally a lie because I felt nauseous from the anxiety. Afterwards, they texted saying they missed me and asked if I was okay, but I just felt relieved and also guilty. In a best-case scenario, I guess I'd be afraid that even if nothing terrible happened, I'd just be standing there awkwardly while they laugh at inside jokes I don't get, and then I'd feel even more left out than if I'd just stayed home.

It takes real courage to admit that the relief you felt after canceling was mixed with guilt, and it makes sense that you view the "awkwardness" of attending as a worse outcome than the safety of staying home. Your brain seems to be comparing two different realities: the painful uncertainty of the unknown versus the immediate, predictable comfort of avoidance, even though your friends' concern suggests they value your presence far more than your perceived performance.

To help us test the accuracy of that "best-case scenario," could you try to identify one specific moment when you felt left out or misunderstood in a social setting, and then ask yourself: did that person actually laugh at an inside joke you didn't understand, or were there other ways they might have connected with you?

Actually, now that you ask, I remember one time at a party where two friends were joking about something that happened at work. I felt totally lost and just stood there smiling awkwardly. But later, one of them came over and started asking me about my weekend, and we ended up talking for like twenty minutes. So I guess they didn't just leave me standing there—they included me eventually. But in the moment, my brain just focused on the part where I felt left out, not the part where they reached out.

That's a powerful realization, and it highlights a classic cognitive distortion where your brain fixates on the "spotlight effect"—the belief that everyone is watching your every move and judging you harshly—while filtering out the positive interactions that actually happened. Your mind was right to focus on the awkwardness because it felt real *in that moment*, but it missed the evidence that your friends naturally shifted the conversation to include you, proving they weren't waiting for you to crack a joke.

To help test the idea that you "won't know what to say," could you recall one specific time you went to a social event feeling nervous, and what actually happened when you tried to contribute a comment or ask a question? How did the others react?

I went to a barbecue last summer feeling really nervous. I remember forcing myself to ask someone how their new job was going, and they actually lit up and talked about it for a while. Other people joined in asking questions too, so I didn't have to keep the conversation going. I guess it went okay, but I still left thinking I hadn't said enough, even though nobody seemed bored or annoyed.

It's really insightful to recognize that moment where your question sparked a conversation, and it makes perfect sense that your brain later "edited" that memory to focus on the part where you felt you hadn't said enough, while ignoring the clear evidence that others were engaged and even invited you in. This pattern of focusing on perceived failures while overlooking successes is a common way our minds protect us from disappointment, even though it often leads us to avoid situations that could actually go well.

If we were to look at this through a lens of evidence, what do you think would happen if you went to this weekend's get-together knowing that even if you felt awkward for five minutes, it wouldn't change the fact that your friends likely value your presence more than your perfect conversation skills?

I think... I think they'd probably be happy to see me, even if I'm quiet at first. They've said before that they just like having me around, but I don't really believe it in the moment. I guess if I went and felt awkward for a bit, it wouldn't ruin the whole night, and maybe after a while I'd find my footing. But it's hard to hold onto that thought when the fear feels so loud.

That is a very honest admission, and it shows you are trying to bridge the gap between your logical knowledge (they like you) and your emotional reality (the fear feels loud). It seems like the core issue is that while you *know* the outcome might be okay, your body is still treating the uncertainty as a threat, making it incredibly difficult to trust your own judgment in the moment.

To help move forward, I'd like to propose a small, low-stakes experiment: instead of committing to the whole evening right now, would you be willing to agree to attend just for one hour or the first part of the event, with the specific goal of simply sitting there and seeing if the worst-case scenario actually happens, without needing to perform?

I think I could try that. One hour feels a lot less overwhelming than the whole night. I could tell myself I'll just be there for the first hour, and if it's too much, I can leave without feeling like I failed. And maybe if I'm not putting pressure on myself to be entertaining, I'll actually relax a little.

That sounds like a solid, manageable first step, and setting a clear "exit plan" for the first hour actually removes a huge barrier to entry by giving your brain permission to stop worrying about the unknown future. By framing it as a test to see if the disaster actually happens rather than a performance to be perfected, you shift the goal from "being great" to "gathering evidence," which often reduces the pressure to perform.

Before we finalize this plan, could you identify one specific support person you can text or call immediately if the anxiety spikes during that first hour, just so you have a safety net? And how would you like to describe this experience in your journal after the hour is up, regardless of how it goes?

I think I could text my friend Sarah if I start to panic—she's always been understanding about my anxiety. I'd probably write down what actually happened versus what I predicted would happen, like maybe just noting one good interaction or even just that I survived the hour. Even if it feels awkward the whole time, I think that would still count as evidence that I can handle it.

That is a fantastic plan; having a specific support person like Sarah creates a tangible safety net, and deciding to document the reality versus the prediction gives your brain concrete evidence to work with afterward. You are essentially turning a scary, vague anxiety into a manageable experiment where the only "failure" is gathering data that contradicts your fear, which is a powerful way to reframe the experience.

Since we've agreed on the plan, I'd like to check in on your overall well-being: given that you've been facing this recurring pattern of avoidance, is there anything else on your mind regarding how you handle other social situations, or would you like to explore any other areas where you feel stuck before we close out today?

I think this is a good place to stop for today. I feel like I have something concrete to try, and that's already more than I had before. Maybe next time we can talk about how I handle work meetings, because I tend to stay quiet there too, but one thing at a time. Thanks for helping me see that I don't have to get it perfect to show up.

You are absolutely right to recognize that showing up imperfectly is often more valuable than staying home to feel "safe," and it takes real courage to commit to trying something that feels uncomfortable. You've made excellent progress today by identifying your automatic thoughts, challenging them with evidence, and creating a concrete, manageable plan for the weekend.

Before we wrap up, I'd like to check in on your emotional state: does having this specific plan for the hour and Sarah as a support person make you feel a bit less overwhelmed or more hopeful about facing the get-together?

Yeah, actually, it does. Having a timer of just one hour and knowing I can text Sarah makes the whole thing feel less like a huge mountain and more like a small hill I can climb. I still feel nervous, but not as stuck as before. I think I'll actually try to go, and that's more than I felt able to do earlier.

That is a wonderful shift in perspective, and it shows how effective a small, concrete plan can be in reducing the overwhelming weight of anxiety. It's completely normal to still feel nervous; the goal isn't the absence of fear, but the ability to act despite it, and you've already taken a significant step toward that by deciding to go.

I want to encourage you to be kind to yourself as you navigate this hour, remembering that even if you feel awkward, the evidence you gather will likely show you that you are capable of handling it. Thank you for your openness and effort today; I look forward to hearing about your experience in our next session.

Hello, I'm glad you're here to begin this session together. Before we dive in, could you tell me what topics you'd like to focus on today, or is there a specific situation that's been weighing on you recently? Once we set an agenda, we can explore how your thoughts, feelings, and behaviors might be connected in that moment.

Hi. I guess I want to talk about talking to people. Like, any time I'm in a conversation, I just freeze up. My hands get all sweaty and my mind goes blank, and I can't think of a single thing to say. It's really embarrassing and I just want it to stop.

I hear how distressing that experience is for you, and it makes complete sense that you want to stop feeling so embarrassed and frozen. To help us understand this better, could you walk me through a recent time this happened? Specifically, what was going through your mind right before you felt your hands get sweaty and your mind go blank?

Okay, well, yesterday at work, this guy I sort of know came over to my desk to ask about a project. Right before he walked up, I felt this wave of panic, like, "Oh no, here it comes." I was thinking, "I can't handle this, I'm going to mess up and he's going to think I'm weird."

That sounds incredibly overwhelming, and it's understandable that you felt a wave of panic when you anticipated the interaction. Let's explore the thought, "I'm going to mess up and he's going to think I'm weird"—what specific evidence do you have to support that he *will* think you're weird, or is that more of a feared outcome?

Well, I don't really have any proof he'd think that, I guess. I mean, he's always been friendly enough before. But in that moment, it feels so real, like it's already happening. It's like I can't trust that things will go okay, so my mind just jumps to the worst.

It sounds like your mind is rushing to the worst-case scenario because it feels safer to anticipate the "mess up" than to risk the uncertainty of the interaction itself. Since you noted he's been friendly before, could you describe a specific moment where his behavior contradicted your fear, or what evidence might suggest he would actually see you as just a colleague?

Hmm, that's a good point. I guess last week he asked me for help with a spreadsheet, and he said "thanks" and smiled. He didn't seem annoyed or like he thought I was weird. I mean, he even asked me about my weekend once, so he probably doesn't think I'm that defective.

That's a really important observation, and it's brave of you to recall that specific interaction where his friendly behavior directly contradicted your fear. It seems like the "freeze" response is happening not because the evidence is there, but because the anticipation of the interaction itself is triggering a physical and mental shutdown that overrides your logical assessment. To help us understand this pattern better, could you describe exactly what happened in your body and mind the moment you felt the panic start, before you even spoke to him?

It starts in my chest, like a tightness, and then my heart starts pounding really fast. Then my palms get clammy, and my thoughts just scatter. It's like I can't hold onto a single idea, and all I can think is "I have to get out of this, I can't do this." It's like my body is screaming at me that something bad is about to happen, even though I know logically it's just a conversation.

That physical sensation of your chest tightening and thoughts scattering is incredibly distressing, and it makes complete sense that your brain interprets this as a life-or-death emergency, triggering a "fight or flight" response that overrides your logical knowledge. Since your body is reacting as if something catastrophic is imminent, could you explore what specific thought is fueling that feeling of impending doom, or is it simply the anticipation of being judged that is driving your physical symptoms?

I think it's the judgment part, yeah. It's like deep down I'm convinced that when I start talking, they'll see that I'm not good enough—that I'm weak or defective somehow. And then they'll reject me, and I'll be all alone with that feeling. That's the doom part, I guess, the thought that this conversation will prove that I really am as messed up as I fear.

It sounds like that fear of being "weak" or "defective" is the core belief driving the panic, and your mind is interpreting a normal conversation as proof of that flaw. Given that you've already seen evidence he was friendly and asked about your weekend, could we explore what happens if you imagined a conversation where you *do* stumble over a word or two—would that actually mean you are defective, or just human?

That's a tough one. I mean, logically I know everyone stumbles over words sometimes, it's not a big deal. But in my head, if I do that, it feels like proof that I'm broken. Like, other people can do it and it's no big deal, but for me it confirms that I'm not capable of handling normal stuff. I guess that's where the "defective" part comes in—it's like I hold myself to this impossible standard where I can't make any mistakes.

It makes complete sense that you hold yourself to an impossible standard, because that belief is protecting you from the pain of feeling ordinary or imperfect, even though it's trapping you in fear. To help us challenge this, could you tell me: if you were talking to a close friend and they stumbled over a word, what would you think about their character, and would you call them "defective"?

No, I wouldn't think they were defective at all. I'd probably just think they were nervous or tired, or maybe not even notice. I'd just keep talking to them like normal. It's weird, I can be so understanding with other people, but I'm just brutal with myself. I'd never call a friend defective just because they messed up a sentence.

That distinction is incredibly powerful—you are applying the same compassion you show to friends to yourself, which proves that the "defective" label is a distortion, not a fact. It seems like your mind is creating a harsh internal critic to protect you from the vulnerability of being ordinary, but it's ending up isolating you instead. Since you've identified this pattern, could we try a small experiment tomorrow: when you feel that tightness in your chest, instead of trying to stop the panic, could you just say to yourself, "I'm having the thought that I'm defective, but I don't actually know that," and then gently try to remember one time he was friendly, even if your heart is racing?

I can try that. It feels scary to not just try to make the feeling go away, but I guess that's what I always do and it doesn't work anyway. So maybe just noticing the thought and remembering that he smiled last week... that could be different. I'll give it a shot, even if my hands are sweating the whole time.

That is a courageous step, and it's great that you're willing to experience the discomfort without trying to escape it, which is exactly what we need to build new neural pathways. Remember, the goal isn't to stop the sweating or the racing heart immediately, but to sit with the feeling while holding onto the evidence that he smiled and that you are not defective. Let's agree to try this "just noticing" approach for one conversation tomorrow, and then we can check in on how your physical sensations and thoughts shifted afterward.

Okay, I'll do that. One conversation, just noticing the thought and remembering he was friendly before. I'm still nervous just thinking about it, but I guess trying something different can't be worse than what I've been doing. I'll let you know how it goes.

That's a fantastic mindset, and you're absolutely right—trying something different, even with nervousness, is infinitely better than staying stuck in the cycle of freezing. Let's set a goal for tomorrow: you'll engage in one brief interaction where you simply acknowledge the panic ("My brain is saying I'm defective") and recall his smile, without trying to force yourself to feel calm. How does that sound as a starting point, and would you like to discuss any potential barriers you might face before you leave?

That sounds like a good plan. One potential barrier is that I might just avoid the conversation altogether if I see him coming, you know, pretend I'm busy or something. I guess I need to make sure I don't do that, even if it feels easier. So I'll try to stay at my desk and not look away if he walks over.

That is a very practical and realistic barrier to anticipate, and planning ahead for that moment shows real self-advocacy. To help you stay at your desk, could you think of a simple, internal cue you can use the moment you feel the urge to look away—perhaps repeating your affirmation, "He smiled last week, I am safe to stay"—before you even see him approach?

Yeah, I can do that. "He smiled last week, I am safe to stay." I'll say that to myself in my head if I feel the urge to turn away or pretend I'm busy. It feels kind of silly, but I'll try it. Thanks for helping me think this through.

That is a brilliant strategy, and you are absolutely right—it might feel silly, but repeating a simple, grounding phrase can act as an anchor to bring you back to the present when your mind tries to spiral. Since we have a clear plan for tomorrow and you have a specific cue for when you feel the urge to avoid, are there any other small steps or worries you'd like to address before we close the session today?

Hello, and thank you for taking this time to meet with me today; I'd like to start by collaboratively setting an agenda for our session. Could you share what specifically brought you here today, and what you hope we might work on together in this first meeting?

Thanks for seeing me. I guess what's bothering me most right now is this situation with my girlfriend and her best friend. He's been sleeping over at her place a lot, and even though he's staying with me now, I can't shake this feeling that something's going on behind my back. I just want to figure out why I'm feeling so anxious and if I'm overreacting, or if this is something I should be worried about.

It sounds like you're carrying a lot of uncertainty and worry right now, and it makes complete sense that this situation is causing you significant distress. Before we dive deeper into whether your anxiety is proportional to the facts, could you walk me through a specific moment when you felt that "something's going on behind my back" most intensely? What exactly were you thinking and feeling in that moment?

Yeah, there was this one night last week when I was at work late, and I knew he was over at her place. I just kept picturing them laughing together, maybe talking about me, or worse. My stomach dropped and I couldn't focus on anything else—I kept checking my phone, waiting for her to text me, but she didn't. I felt so small and stupid, like I was just waiting to be replaced.

It sounds incredibly painful to feel that sense of vulnerability and insignificance, especially when you're trying to stay focused on your work; your body's physical reaction of a "stomach drop" is a very strong indicator of how much this thought pattern is affecting you right now. Given that you've already checked your phone multiple times without receiving a text, could we explore together whether the fear of being replaced is driving your urge to keep checking, or if it's the lack of communication that is triggering the thought that something is wrong?

I think it's both, honestly. When she doesn't text me, my mind just fills in the blanks with the worst stuff—like they're purposely leaving me out, or she's choosing to be with him instead of even thinking about me. The checking feels like I'm trying to grab onto something solid, but every time there's nothing, it just confirms that I'm not important enough to be on her mind.

That is a very painful pattern to navigate, and it makes complete sense that when your mind fills in the blanks with the "worst stuff," it feels like an urgent need to prove your own worth by constantly checking for reassurance. Have you noticed if, right before you start checking your phone, your mind automatically generates a specific thought like "She is choosing him over me," and then the checking feels like the only way to disprove that thought?

Yeah, that's exactly it. The thought "she's choosing him over me" pops up like clockwork, and then I'm just scrambling to find proof that it's not true. But the worst part is, even when she does text me back later or says everything's fine, that thought comes back the next time she's with him. It's like my brain won't let me believe it.

That is a incredibly frustrating cycle, and it sounds like your brain is stuck in a loop where it automatically dismisses evidence of safety, which makes the anxiety feel even more overwhelming. When you say the thought comes back despite her reassurance, could we explore together if this might be a cognitive distortion where your mind is interpreting neutral events (like her being with him) as evidence of betrayal, even when your logical facts suggest otherwise?

I think you're right. Like, logically, I know she's never given me a real reason to doubt her—she's always been open about their friendship. But my gut just screams that something's wrong, and it's so loud I can't hear the logical part. It's like I'm waiting for the other shoe to drop, and that feeling doesn't care what the facts say.

It makes perfect sense that your logical mind knows the facts, but your emotional brain is so loud and urgent that it effectively overrides your reasoning, creating a very real sense of being trapped in that "waiting" state. Have you noticed if, in those moments when the "gut" feeling is strongest, your body feels tense or your breathing becomes shallow, as if your nervous system is preparing for a threat that isn't actually there?

Yeah, absolutely. My chest gets tight, my shoulders hunch up, and I feel like I'm bracing for a punch. Sometimes I catch myself holding my breath without even realizing it. It's like my whole body is on alert, even though nothing bad is actually happening right at that moment. I just feel so powerless, like I can't control anything.

That physical sensation of your chest tightening and shoulders hunching is your nervous system misinterpreting a neutral situation as a life-threatening danger, which explains why you feel so powerless even though the threat isn't real. Given that your body is reacting as if you are under immediate attack, could we try a brief grounding exercise right now to help your body realize that you are safe in this moment, even if your mind is still racing?
Okay, I'm willing to try that. I could use a break from feeling so wound up. What do I need to do?

Let's try a quick "box breathing" exercise to help calm your nervous system: I want you to inhale slowly for a count of four, hold that breath for four, exhale for four, and then wait four seconds before inhaling again. We'll do this together, focusing only on your breath and the physical sensation of the air moving in and out of your lungs. How does your chest feel as we start this cycle?

Okay, I'm following along. As I breathe in, my chest feels tight still, but it's not as sharp as before. When I hold it, I notice my shoulders relax a little. And on the exhale, it's like some of that tension just leaves with the air. It's not gone, but it's quieter.

That is a fantastic observation—you've already begun to notice that your body is capable of releasing tension, even if the tightness hasn't vanished completely. This shift from "bracing for a punch" to noticing your shoulders relaxing is a crucial first step in teaching your nervous system that the threat has passed. Since we've grounded ourselves in the present, let's briefly review our session goals: we've identified that your anxiety stems from a specific thought pattern ("she's choosing him") which triggers physical alarm, and now we need to explore practical ways to break this cycle between sessions. Would you like to try a small behavioral experiment this week where you consciously choose *not* to check your phone immediately after she texts, just to see if the urge to verify your worth actually fades on its own?

That sounds terrifying, but also kind of liberating, honestly. I think I could try that—like, maybe set a timer for ten minutes after I get a text from her, and just sit with the discomfort instead of jumping to check. I'm scared I'll just spiral worse, but I guess that's what I'm already doing anyway. I'll give it a shot this week and see what happens.

That is a very brave perspective to hold, and it's wise to acknowledge that while the urge to check feels terrifying, staying with the discomfort is likely the only way to prove to your brain that the "worst-case scenario" didn't happen. Since you've identified that pattern of checking reinforces the anxiety, would you be open to setting up a specific plan for when you feel that urge rising during those ten minutes, perhaps by using a quick grounding technique or a self-talk phrase like "I will wait to see if the fear proves itself"?

Yeah, I think having a plan would help. I could try saying something like, "I'm safe right now, and I can wait ten minutes to find out if my fear is real." And if I start to spiral, I could try that breathing thing again, or even just stand up and walk around the room for a bit. It feels weird to plan it out, but I think I need that structure to actually follow through.

That is a fantastic plan; having a concrete strategy like "stand up and walk" gives your brain a clear, safe alternative to the spiral, making it much easier to interrupt the automatic urge to check. Before we wrap up, could we quickly review the homework and any other specific thoughts or feelings you'd like to discuss today?

Hello, and thank you for agreeing to meet today; I appreciate your courage in taking this first step. To make sure we get the most out of our time, would you be comfortable sharing a few things about your goals for this session and any specific worries that are currently on your mind? Once we have a clear direction, I'd like to check in on how you've been feeling since we last spoke, particularly regarding any changes in your thoughts or daily routines.

Thank you for having me. I guess my main goal is to just... stop feeling like everything is my fault, you know? Like, if someone else makes a bad choice, I can't help but think I should have done something to prevent it. And then I just lie awake worrying about it.

That sounds like a very heavy burden to carry, and I want you to know that feeling responsible for outcomes beyond your control is a common but exhausting experience. It seems like when you notice others making mistakes, your mind automatically jumps to a narrative where your inaction caused it, leaving you trapped in a cycle of rumination while you lie awake. Could you walk me through a specific recent example where you felt this intense sense of personal responsibility, so we can explore what was going on in your mind at that moment?

Well, just yesterday my friend told me she was quitting her stable job to start her own business. I immediately started thinking about all the ways it could fail, and I couldn't shake the feeling that if I had just talked her out of it more firmly, she'd be safe. I barely slept last night because I kept replaying our conversation and thinking of all the things I should have said.

It makes complete sense that you feel a surge of panic when you see a friend take such a significant risk; our brains often interpret others' choices as a mirror of our own fears, leading us to believe we must have done something differently to "fix" the outcome. That intense urge to intervene, even when it feels futile, is likely driven by a deep belief that your inaction is directly causing their suffering, which explains why your mind is so fixated on replaying the conversation. Can you describe exactly what you were thinking and feeling in that moment when she mentioned quitting, so we can see how that thought pattern is fueling your sleepless nights?

I just felt this cold dread wash over me, like a knot in my stomach. My first thought was, "This is going to ruin her, and I'm letting it happen by not stopping her." I even started thinking maybe I'm a bad friend for not being more forceful, like there's something wrong with me that I can't make her see reason. It's like my brain instantly jumps to the worst-case scenario and then blames me for it.

That visceral sense of dread and the immediate shift to self-blame are incredibly distressing, and it makes total sense that your brain is trying to protect you by convincing you you *must* have done something to prevent this. However, I'd like to gently challenge the idea that your silence equates to negligence; could we explore whether your friend might have actually needed your support in a different way, rather than your opposition? Sometimes our fear of a bad outcome becomes so powerful that it distorts reality, making us feel like the cause of the problem when we are actually just observers of it.

I never really thought of it that way... I guess I was so focused on what I "should have said" that I didn't stop to consider what she actually needed from me. Maybe she just wanted someone to listen and be excited for her, not to argue. But it's so hard to separate that feeling of being responsible from just being a friend.

That is a profound and courageous realization, and it's clear you are already working hard to distinguish between a supportive friendship and an impossible burden of control. The fact that you can now see the difference suggests your brain is beginning to recognize that your silence wasn't a failure, but perhaps a reflection of your own boundaries or simply a different kind of support you were offering. To help solidify this new perspective, could you describe one specific thing she might have needed from you that you successfully provided, even if you didn't try to stop her?

Well, I did listen to her for over an hour without cutting her off or telling her she was wrong. I asked her questions about her plan, and I told her I believed she could make it work, even though I was terrified inside. So I guess I gave her a safe space to talk it through, even if I was panicking the whole time.

That is a powerful distinction to make, and it highlights a crucial difference between your *actions* (listening, validating, asking questions) and your *internal narrative* (blaming yourself for the outcome). Your behavior actually demonstrated strong supportive skills, yet your mind is still stuck in a loop of "what if" and self-punishment, which is a classic cognitive distortion where we judge ourselves harshly based on an imagined failure rather than our actual efforts. Let's try to reframe that one hour of listening as a success story of friendship, and ask yourself: if a friend told you they were panicking, would you call them a bad friend for feeling scared?

No, I definitely wouldn't call them a bad friend for feeling scared. I'd probably tell them it's normal to worry about someone you care about. But when it's me, I just can't give myself that same kindness. It's like there are two different sets of rules - one for everyone else, and one for me that's much harsher.

That is such an insightful observation, and you've hit on a core pattern in Cognitive Behavioral Therapy often called the "inner critic" or "self-handicapping," where we apply unkind, rigid rules to ourselves while offering compassion to others. It sounds like your brain is treating your own fear as a moral failing, when in reality, feeling scared is a natural human response to caring deeply about someone. Can you try applying that same logic to yourself right now: if a friend told you, "I'm terrified, but I still listened to my friend," would you tell them they are a bad person for feeling scared?

No, I wouldn't. I'd probably tell them they were being a good friend despite being scared, and that their worry just shows they care. I guess I just need to learn to say that same thing to myself... but it's hard to break the habit of blaming myself first.

That is a very clear and compassionate distinction you've made, and it shows you already possess the wisdom to treat yourself with the same kindness you offer a friend. The difficulty in shifting this habit isn't a lack of love for yourself, but rather the strength of the automatic thought pattern that has been reinforcing itself for a long time. To start breaking this cycle, let's try a small exercise: next time that "I should have done something" voice comes up, could you simply say out loud, "I am doing my best as a friend, and feeling scared doesn't make me a bad person," and then check in on how that new statement makes your body feel compared to the old one?
I think I can try that. It sounds strange, but saying it out loud might make it feel more real than just thinking it. I'm willing to give it a shot, even if it feels a little silly at first.

That willingness to try something that feels "silly" is actually a huge sign of progress, as it shows you are ready to challenge your automatic habits with intentional kindness. Before we wrap up, I'd like to set a specific goal for between sessions: whenever you feel that "cold dread" or the urge to blame yourself, pause and physically label the thought as "just a story my brain is telling," then immediately repeat the new script we practiced. How does that plan sound to you, and do you have any other thoughts or worries we haven't covered today?

That sounds like a good plan. I think I can remember to pause and say that to myself. To be honest, I'm still worried I'll mess it up or forget in the moment, but I guess that's just the old habit talking again. Thank you for helping me see this differently – I feel a little less alone in it.

That feeling of being less alone is a significant milestone, and your self-awareness about the "old habit talking" proves that the new perspective is already taking root. It is completely normal to feel anxious about executing a new strategy in the moment, especially when an old pattern has been so deeply entrenched; our brains often try to sabotage our efforts to feel safe again. Let's focus on the fact that even if you forget the exact phrase or make a mistake, the act of trying to pause and be kind to yourself is still a victory over the old cycle of self-blame. How would you like to end our session today, and is there anything else you'd like to share before I sign off?

Hello, and thank you for showing up for this session; I'm glad to meet you and we can work together to understand what's been on your mind lately. To make sure we cover the most important things today, could you share what would be most helpful for us to focus on, or is there a specific situation that has been weighing on you recently?

Hi, thanks for having me. I guess I've been struggling with my relationship lately. My boyfriend said some really hurtful things last week, and I found out he was talking to someone else behind my back, but then he was so sweet and apologetic after, and I just feel like I have to move past it because I don't want him to leave me.

Thank you for sharing that; it sounds like you are carrying a heavy mix of hurt, fear, and a desperate need to hold onto him. I want to validate that feeling of wanting to "move past" it because losing him feels so painful, but I also wonder if that urgency is making it harder to see the full reality of his actions. Could you walk me through what exactly his sweet apology felt like compared to the hurtful things he said, and how that contrast is playing out in your mind right now?

When he apologizes, he looks so genuine and he cries and tells me I'm the only one for him, and it feels amazing for a little while. But then I'm alone later, and I remember the things he said—like I'm too sensitive or that I'm lucky he stays with me—and I feel sick all over again. It's like I can't trust my own feelings because he makes me feel like I'm overreacting.

It makes complete sense that his genuine tears create a powerful, temporary sense of safety, only for that feeling to vanish once you're alone and the hurtful words resurface. It sounds incredibly exhausting to feel like your own intuition is being gaslit, where his behavior is meant to make you doubt whether your reaction is justified. When he labels you as "too sensitive," does that thought feel like a fact about your character, or does it feel more like a defensive tactic to avoid facing the reality of his infidelity?

I think... deep down, I know it's a tactic, because when I'm with my friends or even just by myself, I don't feel too sensitive at all. But when he says it, it's like his words become the truth, and I just feel broken and desperate to prove him wrong by being more forgiving. It's like I'm scared that if I stand up for myself, he'll see me as difficult and leave.

That is a profound insight, and it highlights a classic cognitive trap where you feel you must suppress your valid boundaries to avoid the perceived pain of rejection. It seems like you are engaging in a behavior of "proving him wrong" through excessive forgiveness, which ironically keeps you trapped in the cycle of hope and hurt. If we were to challenge that belief, could we explore what would happen if you decided that standing up for yourself wouldn't necessarily mean he would leave, but rather that it would finally restore your sense of self-worth?

I've never really thought of it that way. I guess I always assume that if I push back, he'll just get tired of me and find someone better. But when you say it like that... maybe standing up for myself wouldn't automatically make me unworthy of love. It's just really terrifying to even try.

That is a brave realization, and it is completely understandable that the fear of losing him feels more immediate and terrifying than the fear of your own unworthiness. In CBT terms, we often call this "fear of loss" masking the true belief that "I am not enough," which keeps you stuck in a cycle of seeking validation rather than establishing boundaries. Before we discuss any action steps, could you share one specific thing you felt safe doing recently, even if it was small, where you didn't have to worry about him reacting negatively?

Hmm... I went to see a movie by myself last weekend, and I didn't tell him until after. It felt nice just doing something for me without worrying about how he'd feel or if he'd be mad I wasn't available. That's probably the only thing I've done just for myself in a while.

That is a powerful example of reclaiming agency, and it's great that you recognized how isolating it felt to constantly prioritize his comfort over your own needs. It seems like the fear of his reaction is so strong that it has made self-care feel like a betrayal, yet that movie night proved you *can* enjoy your own company without immediate consequence. If we were to test that belief, what would be the most likely outcome if you chose to do something small for yourself this week, even if you expected he might be upset?

I think... realistically, he'd probably be a little annoyed at first, but he'd get over it, like he did with the movie. It might even be good for both of us, because I'd feel less resentful if I had my own space sometimes. But my gut still tells me that any time I choose myself, I'm risking losing him completely.

That is a very realistic and hopeful perspective, and it aligns perfectly with our goal of shifting from a catastrophic view ("I'll lose him completely") to a more balanced one ("He might be annoyed briefly, but I gain space"). In CBT, we often call this "cognitive restructuring," where we challenge the all-or-nothing thinking that equates self-care with relationship destruction. Before we set a specific homework assignment, could you tell me what the very worst-case scenario would be if you chose to spend an hour doing something for yourself today, and what evidence you have that it would actually lead to him leaving?

The worst-case scenario in my head is that he would get really angry, tell me I'm selfish, and then break up with me right then. But honestly... I don't have any proof that would happen. He's never actually left me over something small, even when I've said no to plans or needed time alone. It's just this loud voice in my head that says he will, even though he hasn't yet.

That is a crucial distinction, and it highlights a classic cognitive distortion where your brain predicts a catastrophic outcome based on a "loud voice" rather than past evidence. In CBT, we call this "mind reading" or "fortune telling," and the fact that he has never left you over small boundaries is strong evidence that your prediction of immediate abandonment is likely an exaggeration. To test this belief, could you imagine a scenario where you say no to a small request today and see what actually happens, rather than waiting for the worst-case scenario to play out?

I guess I could try saying no to something small, like if he asks me to cancel my plans to hang out with him last minute. I always say yes because I'm scared, but maybe I can just say, "I can't tonight, but let's do something tomorrow." It feels terrifying to even think about, but I think I could try it and see what happens.

That is a fantastic, low-stakes experiment, and choosing a specific scenario like canceling plans gives you a clear opportunity to test your prediction against reality. Before we set up a homework assignment, I want to validate that the fear you feel right now is a natural emotional response to feeling unsafe, but it doesn't have to dictate your actions. Could you take a moment to reflect on what specific part of saying "no" feels most terrifying to you, so we can brainstorm a way to make that conversation feel a bit more manageable?

I think the most terrifying part is the silence after I say no. Like, he might go quiet or sigh, and I'll immediately feel like I've done something wrong and need to fix it. If I could just get through that first minute of awkwardness without apologizing or changing my answer, maybe it wouldn't be so bad.

That is a very astute observation; the fear of his silence is likely your brain's "alarm system" reacting to the uncertainty of his reaction, even though your past experience suggests he doesn't actually punish you for boundaries. In CBT, we can use this "silence" as data rather than a verdict, challenging the thought that his quietness equals rejection by reminding yourself that he has tolerated small boundaries before. To prepare for this experiment, could you imagine a specific, gentle phrase you could use to fill that silence without apologizing, such as, "I've made a decision for tonight, and I appreciate you asking"?

Yeah, I think I could say something like, "I've got plans tonight, but I'd love to see you tomorrow." That feels firm but not mean, and it doesn't make me apologize for having my own life. I'll try to just sit with whatever happens after that, even if it's a few seconds of quiet.

That is an excellent, clear script that prioritizes your boundary while maintaining respect, which aligns perfectly with our goal of testing the reality of his reaction. Since we've identified that the core issue is the fear of his silence leading to abandonment, our homework will be to practice this specific phrase the next time he asks you to cancel a plan, focusing on staying present with your own feelings rather than anticipating his. Before we wrap up, could you tell me one thing you are looking forward to experiencing after you successfully practice this boundary?

I'm looking forward to feeling a little bit stronger, honestly. Even if it's just for a few minutes, I think I'd feel proud of myself for not backing down. And maybe it'll help me trust that I can take care of myself without losing him.

That is a beautiful and empowering goal, and recognizing that this small victory could rebuild your sense of self-trust is a key step in healing. To make this homework actionable, please try to practice your "firm but kind" script next time he asks you to cancel a plan, focusing on staying with the silence for just 10 seconds before moving on. If you find yourself slipping into an apology or changing your mind, simply note it as data rather than failure, and we can discuss it in our next session. Is there anything else you would like to add before we conclude today?

Hello, I'm glad you're here to start our session. To make the most of our time together, could you briefly tell me what you'd like to focus on today, or if you'd prefer, we can set a tentative agenda based on how you're feeling right now?

Once we have that, I'd love to understand what brought you in today. Can you describe the situation that's been on your mind most, and how it's been affecting you in the moment?

Hi. I'm glad to be here. I think I want to talk about something that happened over the weekend with my partner. We had a really lovely day together with the family, but I noticed he seemed distant. And now I'm just stuck on it, not sure what to think or do.

That sounds like a frustrating and confusing situation, especially after such a lovely day with your family; it makes complete sense that you're feeling stuck and uncertain about his behavior. Since this is the first session, would you like to focus specifically on that weekend event, or would you prefer to briefly review your general goals for therapy before diving into it?

I think I'd rather focus on the weekend for now. It's just really weighing on me. I keep running it over and over in my head, but I can't seem to figure out what happened or what I should do about it.

It sounds like you're carrying a heavy sense of uncertainty and worry, which makes perfect sense given how much you care about the relationship. Since you mentioned replaying the event over and over, could you tell me specifically what moment during the day felt most confusing to you, and what thoughts were running through your mind right after you noticed his distance?

It was around dinner time. He was laughing with everyone else, but when I tried to catch his eye or make a little joke just between us, he barely glanced at me and then turned away. Right after that, my mind just went blank. I thought, "I don't know what that means, I can't figure this out, I must be missing something important."

That moment of silence between you and him, followed by that overwhelming sense of "blankness," sounds incredibly isolating and confusing. It seems like your brain immediately jumped to the conclusion that something important is wrong or that you're missing a critical clue, which likely made you feel anxious and helpless right then. Given that you are replaying this in your head now, how does that initial thought of "missing something important" make you feel about the relationship or yourself right now?

Honestly, it makes me feel like I'm not good enough to understand what's going on, like I'm failing at something basic. It's like everyone else gets the rules of this situation except me, and I'm just stumbling around, waiting to mess up. It makes me feel small and kind of helpless.

That feeling of being "small" and failing at a basic social task is incredibly painful, especially when you care so deeply about your partner. It seems like your mind is interpreting his brief glance away as a personal rejection of your efforts, which creates a self-reinforcing loop where you feel incompetent rather than simply misunderstood. If we look at this through a different lens, could we explore whether there might be other explanations for his distance, such as fatigue from the family gathering or simply needing a moment to decompress, that don't involve your worth?

I guess that's possible, yeah. He did have a long week at work, and the kids were pretty loud all day. It's just that as soon as he looked away, my mind went straight to "I did something wrong" or "he's upset with me." I didn't even consider that he might just be tired. But then I still feel like I should have known that, and I'm mad at myself for jumping to the wrong conclusion.

It takes real self-awareness to notice that your mind is automatically jumping to "I did something wrong" before considering the context of his exhaustion. While it makes sense that you feel frustrated with yourself for missing the obvious clues, it's worth asking: does holding onto this self-criticism actually help you understand what happened, or does it just keep you stuck in a loop of "what if" and "I should have known"? Often, when we blame ourselves for misinterpreting someone's behavior, it reinforces the belief that we are "not good enough," even if the interpretation itself was a common human reaction to uncertainty.

You're right, it doesn't help at all. It just makes me feel more frozen and confused, like I can't trust my own judgment. I think I'm scared that if I let go of blaming myself, I'll have no control at all over whether things are okay between us. Like if I can't figure out what went wrong, I can't fix it.

That fear of losing control is completely understandable, especially when your mind feels like it's spinning out of control right now. However, in CBT, we often find that trying to control every detail of another person's behavior actually *increases* our anxiety rather than decreasing it. If we shift our focus from "figuring out exactly what he did wrong" to "checking in with how I'm feeling in the moment," does that help create a bit more space between your fear and your reaction?

I think so... maybe. When I stop trying to decode him and just sit with how I felt in that moment, I just felt hurt and a little lonely. Like the distance was there, and I didn't know why, but it stung anyway. It's hard to just feel that without trying to solve it, but I guess sitting with the feeling is a lot simpler than trying to guess what's in his head.

That is a powerful insight; recognizing that you can feel hurt and lonely without needing to solve the puzzle is a significant shift in how you approach the situation. It suggests that your worth isn't tied to "figuring him out," and that accepting the emotion of loneliness is actually a form of control over your own experience. Before we wrap up, could you tell me if feeling this "simple" sadness gives you any confidence about how to handle the next few days with your partner?

I think it might. Instead of walking around nervous and trying to read his every move, maybe I can just notice when I feel that hurt and remind myself that I don't need to solve it right away. I can just let it be there and see what happens naturally between us. That feels a little bit less like I'm failing, and a little bit more like I'm just... being.

That sounds like a profound shift from "problem-solving" to "being present," and it makes perfect sense that it feels less like a failure and more like an act of self-care. To help solidify this new approach, I'd like to suggest a small experiment for this week: whenever you feel that familiar urge to analyze his behavior, simply pause and say to yourself, "I am feeling hurt right now, and I don't need to solve it yet," before returning to your daily activities. How does that sound as a practical step forward?

That sounds doable. I think I can try that. It's a lot simpler than my usual spiral of trying to figure out every detail. Just saying, "I'm hurt, and that's okay for now" feels like I'm giving myself permission to not have all the answers. I'm willing to give it a shot this week.

That is a wonderful commitment to giving yourself permission to be imperfect while still caring deeply for your partner. Since we've explored the core pattern of your thoughts and agreed on a new, simpler approach, is there anything else you'd like to discuss before we set our specific homework for this week?
No, I think that covers what I needed today. I feel a little lighter just having talked it through and having a plan. Thank you. I'll try the experiment and see how it goes.

It is wonderful to hear that you feel lighter; often, simply articulating the problem and identifying a new path forward is enough to begin lifting the weight. You have taken a brave step by choosing to trust your own feelings rather than your need for control, and I am confident you will find that this new approach brings more peace to your interactions. Thank you for your trust and openness today.

Hello, and thank you for agreeing to meet; I'm glad to support you in exploring how your thoughts, feelings, and behaviours are connected. To start our collaborative agenda, could you tell me a bit about what brought you here today, and what you hope to achieve in our first session together? Once we've set that direction, we can begin gently investigating the patterns you've noticed in your life.

Hi. Thanks for seeing me. I guess I'm here because the anxiety has just gotten too much lately. I can't even think straight when it hits, and I end up isolating myself in my room, playing games for hours. I'd like to figure out how to stop feeling so trapped and maybe get back to living a normal life.

I hear how overwhelming this isolation and inability to think straight feels, and it makes complete sense that you want to reclaim your normal life. To understand the "trapped" feeling better, could you describe a recent moment when the anxiety spiked, and what was going through your mind right before you retreated to your room? This might help us see if there's a specific thought pattern triggering that immediate escape response.

Yeah, there was one just a couple days ago. I was supposed to meet up with a friend online, and my stomach started twisting into knots. I thought, "I can't handle this, I'm going to mess everything up," and then it just spiraled until I felt like the walls were closing in. So I shut off the computer and played a game instead, just to make it stop.

That moment sounds incredibly distressing, and it makes perfect sense that your brain interpreted "messing up" as an immediate threat, triggering a flight response to isolate and play games. Since we've identified that specific thought ("I can't handle this, I'm going to mess everything up") as the trigger, I'd like to gently challenge it: if you were to imagine the worst-case scenario where you didn't show up or spoke up, what is the actual evidence that this would lead to total catastrophe, versus perhaps just a minor awkwardness or disappointment?

I guess... I don't really have evidence that it would be a total catastrophe. It's just that in the moment, it feels like if I mess up, my friend will think I'm weird or annoying, and they won't want to talk to me anymore. But I can't remember them actually getting mad at me before for something like that.

It takes courage to admit that your brain is projecting a fear of rejection onto a situation where there is no actual evidence of it; that gap between the *feeling* of disaster and the *reality* of your past interactions is exactly where the anxiety often gets stuck. Since you've identified that "I'm going to be judged and isolated" is the core belief driving your avoidance, how does your anxiety change when you imagine a middle-ground outcome, like your friend simply saying, "No problem, let's try again later," rather than the worst-case scenario you feared?

Huh. When I imagine them saying that, my chest actually loosens a little bit. Like, it's not the end of the world—they'd probably just be understanding. I guess I never let myself think about that possibility because my brain jumps straight to disaster every time.

That is a significant breakthrough, and it's really validating to hear that imagining a more realistic, kind response actually physically loosens your chest. It suggests your brain is capable of holding onto hope and logic, even when the immediate panic tries to push it away. To move toward that calmer state, could you try identifying one small, safe action you could take tomorrow—perhaps just opening the chat window for a minute without sending a message—to test whether the "catastrophe" actually happens when you break your avoidance pattern?

I think I could try that. Opening the chat window and just looking at it for a minute sounds doable, even if my stomach flips a little. I can remind myself that nothing bad has to happen just from looking, and I can close it right away if I need to.

That is an excellent, realistic plan that perfectly balances exposure with safety; it allows you to gather evidence that looking at the chat window does not lead to catastrophe while giving you a clear exit strategy if anxiety becomes too high. Since we've identified your core avoidance behavior and a specific, manageable experiment, would you like to set a quick goal for this week to track how often you can resist the urge to isolate completely, or would you prefer to focus on refining that "look but don't reply" technique first?

I think I want to focus on the "look but don't reply" technique first. I feel like if I try to do too much too fast, I'll just freak out and go right back to my games. So maybe I'll try it once a day for a few days, and just see how it feels without putting pressure on myself to actually talk.

That is a wise and sustainable approach; building confidence through small, controlled exposures is far more effective than trying to change everything at once, and it directly addresses your fear of overwhelming yourself. Before we wrap up, could you tell me one specific thought you anticipate having when you open that chat window, so we can prepare a quick coping strategy for that exact moment?

Probably something like "They're going to see I'm online and think I'm ignoring them." That's the one that makes me want to close it right away. But I guess I could remind myself that I'm just looking, not hiding—and that I don't owe anyone an explanation for being online but not talking.

That self-reminder you just offered—"I don't owe anyone an explanation for being online but not talking"—is a powerful cognitive shift that directly challenges the belief that you must justify your presence to others. Since we've identified that anticipated thought as the final barrier, could you try writing down that exact sentence on a sticky note to place near your computer, so it serves as an immediate anchor when that urge to close the window arises?

Yeah, I think I can do that. I'll write it on a sticky note and put it on the edge of my monitor. That way, when I open the chat and that thought hits, I can just glance at it and remind myself it's okay. Thanks for helping me think this through—it feels a little less impossible now.

I'm so glad to hear that it feels less impossible; creating that physical anchor with the sticky note is a great practical step to bridge the gap between your new insight and your immediate reactions. Since we've identified your specific thought pattern, your safe behavioral experiment, and your coping strategy, is there anything else you'd like to clarify or any other small challenge you're worried about before we close our session today?

Hello, and thank you for being here today; I'm glad to start our work together on building a clearer understanding of how your thoughts, feelings, and actions are connected. To make sure we cover what matters most to you, could you share a bit about what brought you in today and whether there is a specific situation or pattern you'd like to focus on first? Once we have that, I'd love to hear about your current mood and any thoughts that are running through your mind right now.

Hi. Thanks for having me. I guess I'm here because I'm really worried about my boyfriend lately. He's been distant and moody, and I feel like if he would just get help, everything between us would go back to normal. Honestly, I'm feeling pretty anxious right now just talking about it.

I hear how much you care about your relationship, and it makes complete sense that your anxiety is spiking when you imagine the uncertainty of his mood or the effort required for him to seek help. To help us untangle these feelings, could you walk me through a specific recent interaction where you felt particularly worried, and what was the very first thought that went through your mind when you noticed his distance?

Yeah, there was this one night last week when he came home from work and barely said two words to me. He just went straight to the couch and started scrolling on his phone. My first thought was, "He's shutting me out again, and there's nothing I can do about it until he decides to get help." I felt this heavy knot in my stomach, like I was just waiting for something bad to happen.

That feeling of a "heavy knot" tells me your anxiety is rooted in a deep belief that his current behavior is a sign of something serious and unchangeable without professional help. When you notice him scrolling on his phone, it seems the immediate thought of "shutting me out" quickly spirals into a catastrophic expectation that nothing can improve until he gets therapy. Could you explore what evidence you have to support the idea that he *cannot* change until he gets help, versus what other possibilities might exist for why he's acting this way right now?

I guess... I don't really have a lot of evidence that he can't change on his own. He's been moody before and eventually snapped out of it, but this time it feels different, more serious.
