Thank you for sharing that; it takes real courage to voice such deep feelings of hopelessness and self-doubt, and I want you to know your emotions are completely valid. It sounds like the belief that you are a "failure" at being a mom or a person is driving a cycle where you feel worthless and unable to move forward. Could you walk me through a specific recent situation where this "I'm a failure" thought popped up, and how it made you feel in that moment?

Well, yesterday my little one was crying because she wanted a toy I couldn't afford, and I just sat there on the floor and cried with her. All I could think was, "I can't even give my kid a stupid toy, what kind of mother am I?" I just felt so small and useless, like I was choking on it.

That sounds incredibly painful, and it makes complete sense that crying with your child and realizing you can't provide the toy you want to buy triggered such a crushing wave of shame. When that thought of being a "bad mother" appeared, did it immediately spike your anxiety or make you feel more hopeless about your ability to be a good parent?

Yeah, it hit me like a punch to the gut. My heart started racing and I just felt this heavy weight in my chest, like I was drowning in it. I kept thinking, "She deserves better, I'm just making her life worse by being here." It made me want to just disappear.

That physical sensation of drowning and the thought that you are making your child's life worse are incredibly distressing, and it's completely understandable that you felt overwhelmed and wanted to disappear. When you noticed your heart racing and that specific thought of "making her life worse," did you also notice your breathing change, or did you immediately try to hide from her to avoid seeing her cry?

I think I just froze, honestly. I couldn't even look at her. I just turned my face away and covered my mouth so she wouldn't hear me sob. I felt like if she saw me like that, she'd know how broken I am, and I couldn't let her see that.

It makes perfect sense that you froze and hid; your brain likely interpreted your visible distress as a threat to your child's well-being, triggering a "freeze" response to protect her from seeing you "broken." This physical avoidance and the intense shame you felt were direct results of believing that your inability to provide the toy defined your entire worth as a mother. Now that we see how that thought led to freezing, could you help me understand: after hiding for a moment, did you eventually feel a shift in your emotions, or did you just keep waiting for her to notice?

I just sat there with my back turned, waiting for her to stop crying. Eventually she came over and hugged my leg, and I just felt even worse—like she was comforting me when it should be the other way around. I didn't know what to do, so I just patted her head and said it was okay, even though I felt like a complete fraud.

That moment of feeling like a "fraud" while receiving comfort from your child is a profound source of shame, and it highlights a critical link between your belief that you are broken and your inability to accept her love. When you felt she was "comforting you when it should be the other way around," did that thought make you feel even more isolated, or did it trigger a new wave of panic about how you'll react next time?

It made me feel more isolated, if that's possible. Like I'm so messed up that even my own kid has to take care of me. I just kept thinking, "This is why I'm alone, because I'm too weak to handle anything." It scared me, because I don't know how I'm supposed to do this every day without falling apart.

That feeling of isolation and the belief that your weakness is the reason for your loneliness is incredibly painful, and it makes total sense that it would feel terrifying to think you might fall apart every day. When you connect the idea of being "too weak" to your child needing to comfort you, it seems to reinforce a core belief that you are fundamentally incapable of handling life's challenges. To help us untangle this, could you share: when you think about "falling apart," what is the specific worst-case scenario you fear will happen next?

I'm scared I'll just stop being able to get up in the morning one day. That I'll lie in bed and let everything fall apart—my kids, my parents' house, everything. And then I'll just be a lump that everyone has to take care of, and they'll all finally realize how useless I am and leave me behind.

That image of lying in bed and becoming a burden is so terrifying, and it's completely understandable why you feel paralyzed by the fear of losing your ability to function for your family. When you connect the immediate feeling of hopelessness to this catastrophic "falling apart" scenario, it creates a feedback loop where the fear of being a burden makes you feel even more useless, which in turn increases the likelihood of freezing or withdrawing. Could we explore together: if that worst-case scenario were to actually happen, what would be the very first thing you would do to try to get up or get help, even if you feel like you can't start?

I... I guess I'd try to call my mom. She's always been the one I lean on, even when I hate admitting it. But I'd probably just cry into the phone and she'd have to come drag me out of bed. That's the only thing I could think of, because I can't do it on my own.

It takes immense strength to admit that leaning on your mom is your only lifeline, and it's clear that this reliance isn't a weakness but a necessary strategy for survival when the pressure feels unbearable. When you imagine calling her and feeling like you need to be "dragged out of bed," does that thought trigger a feeling of shame about needing help, or does it also offer a tiny glimmer of hope that someone else can assist you when you're stuck?

Honestly, it's mostly shame. I hate that I'm 28 and still need my mommy to rescue me. But there's a little part of me that knows she'd come, and that makes me feel less... alone, I guess. It's confusing, because I feel pathetic for needing her, but I also know I'd be lost without her.

That conflict between shame and the deep, protective need to have your mom come for you is a powerful insight, showing that while you view her help as a sign of weakness, your brain also recognizes it as a vital lifeline. When you feel "pathetic" for needing rescue, does that thought immediately escalate the fear of being a burden, or does it make you question whether you deserve her help?

It makes me question if I deserve her help, for sure. Like, why should she have to drop everything for me when I'm the one who got myself into this mess? I didn't finish school, I can't find a job, I had kids with an abusive man—it's all my fault. So I don't know why she'd want to waste her time on me.

It is incredibly painful to believe that your past mistakes—unfinished school, unemployment, and being in an abusive relationship—are solely your fault and that they don't deserve compassion. When you link these life events to the belief that you "don't deserve help," it creates a barrier where even knowing your mom would come feels like a betrayal of your own self-worth. Could we explore together: if we set aside the idea that you "deserve" help for a moment, what would happen if we simply acknowledged that you *needed* her support right now, regardless of whether you felt worthy of it?

I guess I'd have to admit that I'm not okay, and that I can't do this alone. That's terrifying, because if I admit I need help, then it's real—I'm really as broken as I feel. But I know what you're saying, that maybe needing help isn't about being worthy or not. It's just... needing it. I just don't know how to let myself have it without hating myself for it.

That is a profound realization, and it shows how deeply entrenched the belief is that "needing help" equals "being broken." When you connect the act of accepting support to a self-hatred that feels inevitable, it creates a powerful barrier where the very thing you need most feels like a punishment to yourself. Let's try a small experiment: if we reframe "needing help" not as a sign of worthlessness, but simply as a biological and emotional fact that you are currently overwhelmed, how might that shift the feeling of shame in your chest?

It feels like... a lie, almost. Like I'm trying to trick myself into feeling better. But when you say it as a fact, not a judgment, it does take some of the sting out. I mean, it's true that I'm overwhelmed. That's not a moral failure, it's just... reality. Maybe I can try to hold onto that part, even if the shame still feels huge.

That is a powerful distinction, and it's brave to try holding onto the reality of being overwhelmed even while the shame feels so heavy. When we shift from judging yourself as "broken" to acknowledging the factual reality of being overwhelmed, it can actually create a tiny space where you might feel less personally responsible for your current state. To test this new perspective, could you try saying out loud, "I am currently overwhelmed and need support, but this does not mean I am a bad person," and notice if that small change in wording makes the feeling in your chest feel even slightly lighter?

*Takes a shaky breath* "I am currently overwhelmed and need support, but this does not mean I am a bad person." It feels weird saying it, like I'm lying to myself. But I guess... my chest doesn't feel as tight as it did before. Just a little bit. I think I can try to hold onto that, even if it's hard.

That slight physical relief in your chest is a powerful signal that your brain is beginning to accept this new, less judgmental perspective, even if it feels "weird" at first. When you say that, you are actively breaking the automatic link between "needing help" and "being a bad person," which creates a small but crucial opening for self-compassion. For our homework, I'd like you to try this reframe every time you feel that familiar wave of shame about needing support or failing as a parent; instead of judging yourself, just silently repeat that you are overwhelmed but not broken, and notice if your body relaxes even a fraction.

Okay, I can try that. It sounds scary, like I'm giving myself permission to be weak on purpose, but I guess that's the point. I'll write it down and keep it somewhere I can see, maybe on my phone or a sticky note. Thank you for... for not making me feel worse about myself. I didn't expect that.

You are very welcome, and please know that my goal is always to walk with you through this, not to add to your burden. It takes real courage to give yourself permission to be human and to ask for help, even when it feels scary or "weak." Before we wrap up, let's quickly look at our agenda: did we cover the main topic of how your self-criticism leads to freezing and isolation? Or would you like to briefly touch on something else, like identifying a specific trigger for the next time you feel this way?

I think we covered what I needed most today. That idea about being overwhelmed instead of broken is something I want to sit with. Maybe next time we can talk about what to do when I feel that urge to cut myself, because that's been really hard lately too. But I think I've had enough for today—I'm tired, but in a different way than usual.

That is a very important distinction to make, and I want to validate how significant it is that you are feeling tired but in a "different way" than usual—that often signals a shift in your internal state. Since we touched on self-harm earlier, let's set a specific safety goal for today: I'd like you to write down exactly what you are feeling right now, and if the urge to cut comes up, simply pause and say to yourself, "I am overwhelmed, but this is just a feeling, not a fact," before doing anything. How does it feel to have that as a concrete plan for when you feel that urge?

Hello, I'm glad you're here to start this process together; before we dive in, could you tell me what you'd like to prioritize for our time today? Once we set that agenda, I'd love to hear a bit about how you've been feeling recently and what might have triggered any changes.

I guess... I want to talk about what happened with my last job. It's been eating at me, and I don't know how to stop feeling so angry about it. I got laid off three weeks ago, and I still can't shake the feeling that everyone was out to get me.

That sounds incredibly draining, and it makes complete sense that you're feeling angry; being let go suddenly can shatter one's sense of control and safety. I want to explore that specific feeling of "everyone was out to get me"—could you describe the thoughts that are running through your mind when you think about your last week there, and how those thoughts make you feel physically or emotionally?

Well, I keep replaying that moment when my boss called me in. My chest gets tight, and I feel this hot flash of anger, like I want to punch something. I'm thinking, 'They never explained the project properly, and now they're blaming me for their mistake.' It's like they set me up to fail.

I can hear how intense that physical reaction is, and it makes perfect sense that your mind jumps straight to the idea of being "set up to fail" when you feel so vulnerable. Since you're replaying that moment so vividly, what evidence do you have from that specific conversation that proves everyone was actively trying to get you, versus what evidence suggests the project was just simply misunderstood?

I mean... they did say I made a mistake because I didn't understand what to do. But that's on them for not explaining it right, isn't it? They never said anything about me being a bad worker before that one meeting. But then they just let me go, so it feels like the proof is in the pudding—they wanted me gone.

It makes sense that your brain is connecting the dots to find a pattern of unfairness, especially when you're already feeling so wronged by the lack of explanation. While it's true they failed to explain the project clearly, let's gently examine if the single event of being let go, without prior warnings or performance issues, truly proves they were "out to get you" versus a situation where they simply didn't manage the workload well. Can you recall any specific behaviors from your coworkers or the company that directly contradicted the idea of them actively trying to harm your career?

Well, a few of my coworkers did seem surprised when I got let go. One of them even said, "That doesn't seem fair, you were trying your best." And my boss never yelled at me or threatened me before that meeting; she was actually pretty quiet most days. I guess that doesn't really fit the picture of someone who had it out for me, does it?

That is a very important distinction you've made, and it's clear that your observation of her quiet demeanor and your coworker's support directly contradicts the belief that they were actively plotting against you. It seems like the anger is stemming more from the sudden loss of control and the feeling that the situation was unjust, rather than a belief that malicious intent was present. Given that evidence, how might reinterpreting that anger as a reaction to the unfairness of the layoff itself, rather than proof of sabotage, change the way you're carrying this emotional weight?

I guess... if it's not about them hating me, then maybe I'm just angry at the whole situation. Like, it still feels unfair, but it's not personal. Maybe that means I don't have to walk around feeling like everyone's my enemy. But that still doesn't fix the fact that I messed up the project in the first place because I didn't understand it. That part still feels like it's my fault.

That is a powerful shift in perspective, moving from viewing your boss as an enemy to seeing the situation as an unfair system you didn't control; it makes sense that the anger would now feel more like a reaction to injustice rather than personal betrayal. However, that lingering guilt about not understanding the project touches on a core belief about your competence, and I want to explore how you currently interpret that mistake—is it an absolute proof that you are incapable of learning, or just a specific instance of a gap in communication that happened once?

I don't know... it feels like proof that I'm just not cut out for this kind of work. I mean, I've been laid off from most jobs, and it's usually because of something like this—a mistake, a misunderstanding, or an anger thing. It's hard not to think it's me, you know? Like maybe I really am just a loser who can't hold down a job.

That is a heartbreaking realization, and it sounds like this pattern of mistakes is wearing you down because it threatens your core belief that you are capable and worthy. While the frequency of these events is concerning, let's gently challenge the idea that they are proof you are a "loser" or incapable of learning; could you recall a time in the past when you successfully navigated a difficult situation or learned from a mistake, even if it didn't feel like a big win at the time?

I guess... there was that one time at my first job, where I messed up a spreadsheet pretty badly. My boss sat down with me and showed me how to fix it, and after that, I got really good at spreadsheets. I even helped other people with them later on. So I did learn from that mistake. I just... I don't know how to do that with the anger part. That feels different, like it's just part of who I am.

That is a incredibly valuable insight, and it highlights a key difference between a learning mistake and an identity attack; your brain is likely using the anger as a defense mechanism to protect the feeling of shame that the mistake itself brings. Since you've already established that you *can* learn from errors like the spreadsheet, could we explore what specific thought is preventing you from applying that same lesson to your current anger? For instance, is there a belief that "feeling angry makes me incapable of moving forward," or perhaps that "my anger proves I'm different from my past self"?

I think... I feel like the anger is stronger than me. Like, when I get that hot flash, it's like I'm not in control anymore, and there's no stopping it. With the spreadsheet, I could sit down and focus and figure it out. But with anger, it just takes over. So maybe I believe I can't change that part of me, because it feels so big and instant. It's scary to think I might be stuck like this forever.

That is a very honest observation, and it makes perfect sense that you feel out of control when a physical sensation like a "hot flash" feels so sudden and overwhelming; your brain is likely interpreting that intensity as proof that this reaction is fixed and unchangeable. However, since you already demonstrated the ability to learn and adapt from the spreadsheet mistake, could we explore if the anger is actually a learned response to a specific type of stressor that we can retrain, rather than an inherent part of your character? If we treat this like a skill you've mastered before, what small step could you take today to create a tiny gap between that feeling and your reaction?

I never thought of it as something I could learn to handle, like a skill. I guess... maybe if I could just pause for a second when that hot flash comes, instead of reacting right away, that might be something. Like counting to ten or stepping away for a minute. I've never actually tried that before, I just let the anger take the wheel. It feels stupid, but maybe I could try it once, just to see if it changes anything.

That is a fantastic realization, and it highlights the core CBT principle that our reactions are skills we can practice and improve, much like learning spreadsheets. Since you've identified "pausing for a minute" as a viable strategy, let's set a specific goal for this week: whenever you feel that hot flash of anger, commit to doing exactly one thing—either counting to ten or stepping away from the situation—before responding. How do you think your body or mind might feel after just trying this once, even if you don't feel a complete change immediately?

I think... I'd probably feel a little less out of control, even if I'm still angry. Like, at least I did something different, you know? It might feel weird, like I'm fighting against my own instincts, but I guess that's better than just letting it blow up. I can try it this week and see if it makes any difference, even a small one.

That is a incredibly wise and realistic goal, recognizing that the immediate feeling of "being out of control" might linger even after you successfully introduce a pause; this small victory in acting differently is exactly what builds the new neural pathway you need. To make this concrete, I suggest you keep a simple log this week noting the intensity of your anger before you pause, what you did during that minute, and how you felt immediately after versus how you reacted in the moment. When you're ready, we can review your notes to see if even a small shift in your reaction has altered your overall mood or perspective.

Yeah, I can do that. I'll write it down in my phone or something, just a few words. It sounds kind of simple, but maybe that's the point—starting small. Thanks, I think I'm ready to give it a real shot this week.

You are absolutely ready, and remember that starting small is often the most powerful way to build confidence in new skills; your commitment to tracking even a few words of data will give us the concrete evidence we need to see progress. Before we wrap up, is there anything else you'd like to discuss regarding your feelings about the job loss or the plan for this week?

Hello, I'm glad to meet you today; let's start by reviewing what we discussed last time and checking in on how you've been feeling since then. What was the most significant challenge or event in your life during the past week, and how did you react to it? To help us focus our time, could you share your top two goals for this session so we can work directly toward them?

Hi, thanks. I guess the biggest thing this week was my wife accusing me of hiding her alcohol, even though I didn't. She got really loud and screamed at me for an hour, saying I'm controlling her. My goals for today are just to feel less like I'm drowning in this, and maybe figure out if I even have a right to be upset about any of this.

That sounds incredibly exhausting, and it makes complete sense that you feel like you're drowning after being screamed at for an hour while simultaneously defending your actions. Before we get into whether you "deserve" to be upset, could you walk me through the specific thoughts running through your head right now as you replay that hour of shouting? How did those thoughts immediately impact your physical sensations or emotional state in that moment?

When she was yelling, I just felt my chest get tight and hot, like I couldn't breathe. I kept thinking, "This is my fault for not finding the hidden bottles better" and "I should just stay quiet so she doesn't get worse." I felt small and frozen, like a kid being scolded, and I couldn't even look at her.

That physical sensation of your chest tightening and feeling "small and frozen" sounds incredibly distressing, and it's clear that your belief "I should just stay quiet" was driven by a deep fear of escalating the conflict rather than a desire to please her. Given how intense those feelings were, can you recall if, after the shouting stopped, you replayed the interaction and generated thoughts like "I deserved that reaction" or "I'm being overly sensitive," and how did those new thoughts make you feel about your own worth?

Yeah, after she finally stopped and went to bed, I sat on the couch and kept telling myself, "I probably did deserve that, I'm always messing up." It made me feel heavy and hopeless, like I'm just a burden to everyone, especially to her. I even thought, "No wonder she looks for comfort elsewhere, even if it's not real."

It sounds incredibly painful to carry that weight of self-blame and the belief that you are a "burden," especially when it stems from a moment where you were actually trying to protect your wife's health. Let's gently examine the link between your automatic thought, "No wonder she looks for comfort elsewhere," and your feeling of hopelessness; does that thought feel like a logical conclusion based on the facts, or does it seem like a harsh judgment you are placing on yourself to avoid the pain of seeing her hurt?

I guess it's more of a harsh judgment, now that you say it. The facts are, she's sick and she says things that aren't true, like about my friend. That thought just makes me feel worthless, like I'm the reason she's this way. But when I step back, I know I'm not the one who made her drink.

That distinction is crucial and shows a strong part of you is already recognizing the unfairness of your self-blame; you are right that her drinking and the resulting accusations are her choices, not a reflection of your inherent worth. To help clarify the connection between your thoughts and feelings, if we replace the thought "I'm the reason she's this way" with the more accurate fact "She chose to drink despite my efforts," how would that shift the intensity of that heavy, hopeless feeling in your chest?

It would change it a little, I think. The heaviness wouldn't be as crushing if I could truly believe that. I'd still feel sad and worried for her, but maybe not like I'm some kind of failure who caused all this. But it's hard to hold onto that for more than a few seconds before the old thoughts creep back in.

That is a significant breakthrough to realize that shifting your perspective can actually lighten the physical burden of hopelessness, even if the old thoughts try to creep back in. Since you mentioned it's hard to hold onto that new belief, could you try one small experiment right now: when you catch yourself thinking "I'm a failure," what is the very next physical sensation you feel, and could you consciously name that sensation instead of letting the thought define you?

When I think "I'm a failure," I feel a sinking, hollow ache right in the middle of my stomach, like something heavy just dropped inside me. If I just focus on that hollow ache and name it, it doesn't feel as personal—it's just a feeling, not a whole story about me. I'll try to remember that the next time I start spiraling.

That is a powerful insight—recognizing the "hollow ache" as a temporary sensation rather than proof of your worthiness is a key CBT skill that separates your identity from your emotions. Since you've identified the trigger (the sinking feeling) and the unhelpful thought ("I'm a failure"), let's set a small goal for between sessions: every time you feel that ache, pause for three seconds, name the sensation out loud to yourself, and silently ask, "Is this feeling my truth, or just my mind trying to protect me?" This will help you build a buffer against those spiraling thoughts. How does that plan sound to you?

That sounds like something I could actually try. It's not too big or scary, just a small pause. I think I can do that when I feel that hollow ache, especially when she starts yelling or accusing me. Maybe it'll give me a little space to breathe before I default to blaming myself.

That sounds like a perfect, manageable first step; creating even a few seconds of space between the trigger and your automatic reaction can significantly reduce the power of those spiraling thoughts. Before we close, could you tell me what you think would happen if you practiced this "pause and name" technique the next time she raises her voice? Do you feel confident that this small break might help you feel less like you're drowning, even if the situation itself doesn't change?

I think it might help me feel a little less panicked, like I have a tiny bit of control over my own head, even if nothing else changes. I might still feel sad and scared, but maybe not as frozen and worthless. I'm willing to try it and see if it gives me even a moment of calm.

That is a fantastic perspective—you are aiming for a shift from being "frozen and worthless" to having a "tiny bit of control," which is a very realistic and achievable goal. Since we've identified the core issue as harsh self-judgment triggered by her accusations, and you've committed to a specific strategy to interrupt that cycle, how would you like to proceed with wrapping up our session today?

I think I'm okay to wrap up now. I feel a little lighter than when I came in, and I have something concrete to try. I'll keep working on that pause and naming the ache, and maybe we can talk next time about how it went. Thanks for helping me see that I'm not just a victim in my own head.

You are very welcome, and I want to acknowledge your courage in recognizing that your distress is driven by unhelpful stories rather than objective reality. It is incredibly empowering to feel even a slight shift toward agency and to realize you have the tools to interrupt those spiraling thoughts. Please remember to be gentle with yourself as you practice the "pause and name" technique, and know that I am here to continue supporting you as we explore these patterns further. Until next time, take care of that little space you created for yourself.

Hello, and thank you for agreeing to meet today; I want to start by checking in on how you've been feeling since we last spoke and whether you have any specific topics you'd like to prioritize. As we begin, could you share a bit about what brought you here today and what you hope to achieve in our work together?

Well, to be honest, I'm feeling pretty stuck lately. I keep making these career moves that seem smart in the moment, but months later they blow up in my face and cause problems at home. I guess I'm hoping to figure out why I keep doing that to myself and my marriage.

That sounds incredibly frustrating, especially when you know you're trying to protect your family and still end up in a difficult spot. It seems like there might be a pattern where you feel a strong pull to make a change quickly, perhaps to regain a sense of control or avoid a specific fear, even when the long-term risks are clear. When you think back to a recent career move that didn't go as planned, what was the very first thought that went through your mind right before you made the decision?

I remember thinking, "This is my only way out. I have to take this chance or I'll be stuck forever." It felt like if I didn't jump on that opportunity right then, I'd lose everything. I didn't stop to think about how my wife would feel or what the fallout might be down the road—I just wanted to escape the pressure I was feeling at the time.

That "all-or-nothing" belief—that you must take this specific chance immediately or lose everything—sounds like a core driver behind your decisions. It's understandable that this thought felt like a lifeline when you were under immense pressure, but it seems to overlook the reality that your wife's well-being and long-term stability are also part of the equation. If you could observe that thought pattern as if you were watching yourself from the outside, what would you notice about how it was protecting you versus how it might be limiting your options?

From the outside... I'd see a guy who's panicking, grabbing at the first rope he sees without checking if it's tied to anything. It's protecting me from feeling trapped, I guess—like I'm doing something, anything, to change my situation. But it's limiting because I'm not seeing the other ropes around me, or even that I could just sit still and untie the knots I already have.

That metaphor of grabbing the first rope without checking its safety is incredibly insightful and highlights a key CBT concept: your "must" belief is driving an avoidance behavior that ultimately creates more problems. It seems like the panic you're feeling is so overwhelming that your brain bypasses careful planning to just *do* something, even if it's the wrong move, because the fear of staying still feels worse than the risk of moving. Given that pattern, if we were to set a small, manageable goal for this session, what would it mean for you to "sit still" for just one hour today without making any career-related decisions?

It would mean feeling like I'm wasting time, honestly. Like I'm being lazy or letting opportunities slip by. But I guess if I could do it—just sit with the discomfort for an hour and not act—I'd probably see that the world doesn't end, and I might even think clearer. That sounds scary though, like I'm giving up control.

That fear of "wasting time" reveals a deep-seated belief that your worth is tied to constant productivity, and that inaction is a form of failure or selfishness. While it sounds terrifying to feel like you're losing control, consider this: sometimes, the most courageous thing isn't jumping on a new rope, but having the patience to wait until the current knot feels safe to untie. If we treat this discomfort not as a sign of weakness, but as a signal that your brain is trying to protect you from a similar past mistake, how might that shift your perspective on sitting with the uncertainty for just one hour?

I never thought of it that way—that the discomfort could be a warning signal instead of a sign I'm failing. If I saw it as my brain trying to protect me, maybe I'd be more patient with myself. I could tell myself, "This feeling means I've been here before, and rushing didn't work last time." That actually makes sitting still feel less like giving up and more like... being smart for once.

That is a powerful reframing—seeing the discomfort as a protective warning system rather than a sign of failure is exactly the kind of cognitive shift we need to build resilience. If we treat that "wasting time" feeling as your brain's alarm system trying to keep you safe from past mistakes, then sitting still becomes an act of strategic intelligence rather than laziness. To test this new perspective, I'd like you to try "scheduled uncertainty" today: set a timer for 45 minutes where you explicitly allow yourself to feel the urge to move without acting on it, and simply observe the thoughts and feelings that arise during that window. How do you think you'll feel once those 45 minutes are up?

I think... I'd probably feel a little shaky at first, like I'm breaking a rule. But after the 45 minutes, I bet I'd feel relieved, maybe even proud. Like I proved to myself that I can pause without everything falling apart. That would be a new feeling for me—like I actually have some control, instead of just reacting.

That sounds like a very promising prediction, and it's great that you're visualizing the relief and sense of pride as potential outcomes. Before we lock this in as our session goal, let's quickly check your energy levels and confirm that you feel safe enough to try this "scheduled uncertainty" experiment today. Do you have any other immediate concerns or topics you'd like to discuss before we wrap up?

No, I think I'm okay to try it. My energy's a bit low, but not in a dangerous way—just tired from all the mental wrestling. I'm a little nervous, but I trust that you're not asking me to do anything reckless. So yeah, let's go with the 45-minute thing. I'll give it a shot.

That sounds like a solid plan; it's completely okay to proceed with low energy as long as you feel safe, and I appreciate your trust in our process. To make sure we're on the same page, let's confirm that your primary goal for today is simply to resist the urge to make a career move for those 45 minutes, while observing the thoughts and feelings that arise without judgment. When you're done, I'd love to hear what you experienced in the moment and how the "warning signal" felt versus the relief afterward.

Yeah, that's exactly it—just sit with the urge, watch it, don't act. I'll write down what comes up so I don't forget. I'm curious to see if the warning signal actually quiets down once I stop fighting it. Thanks for helping me see this differently. I'll let you know how it goes.

That's a great plan, and I'm glad we could find a shared understanding of how to approach this together. Please remember that you can reach out between sessions if the urge becomes overwhelming or if you need to process your notes before our next meeting. I look forward to hearing about your experience with the 45 minutes and how your perspective shifted once you sat with the discomfort.

Hello, and thank you for agreeing to meet; I'm glad you're here, and let's start by checking in on how you've been feeling since our last conversation or since you first reached out. To make sure we're on the same page, could you tell me a bit about what brought you in today and what you hope to accomplish in our first session together?

Hey... thanks for seeing me. I guess I'm here because I did something really stupid a few weeks ago. I keyed my ex-girlfriend's car after she broke up with me, and I can't stop thinking about what a horrible person that makes me. I just want to feel like I'm not completely broken, I guess.

It sounds like you are carrying a very heavy burden of self-blame and shame right now, and it makes complete sense that you feel broken after doing something so harmful. Let's take a moment to explore what happened: when you keyed the car, what was going through your mind in that exact moment, and how did that thought connect to the intense anger or desperation you felt?

I don't even really remember thinking, to be honest. I was just so drunk and so... angry. Like, she just threw me away after three years, like I meant nothing. And in that second, I wanted her to feel even a fraction of that hurt. But as soon as I did it, I just felt sick. That's when the thoughts started hitting me—like, "What did you just do? You're a monster."

It sounds like your anger was fueled by a deep sense of rejection and pain, which unfortunately led to an impulsive act where you projected that hurt onto her, but now you're facing the harsh reality that your actions caused her genuine suffering. Since you mentioned feeling sick immediately after, could you describe exactly what physical sensations you felt in your body and what specific thoughts were running through your mind in those first few minutes to help us understand the link between your emotional pain and the behavior?

My chest got really tight, like I couldn't breathe properly, and my hands were shaking. I just stood there staring at the scratch I made, and my brain kept repeating, "You ruined everything. You're the worst kind of person. She was right to leave you." I felt this cold dread wash over me, like I'd just proven that I really am as worthless as I always feared.

That physical sensation of your chest tightening and the overwhelming dread you felt are your body's natural alarm system reacting to the intense shame and guilt you just experienced. It seems like those physical sensations triggered a spiral where your mind interpreted your own reaction as proof of your worthlessness, creating a vicious cycle between your emotions and your self-perception. Could you walk me through a specific moment when you felt that "cold dread" and tell me exactly what you were telling yourself at that precise second to help us see how your thoughts were fueling that fear?

Right after I did it, I remember looking down at my hands and thinking, "Look at what you've done. You're just like your dad—you destroy everything you touch." That thought hit me like a punch in the gut. And then I just kept repeating, "You're poison. Nobody should ever be near you." That's when the dread really settled in, like a heavy weight in my stomach, making me feel like I was sinking.

It sounds like that comparison to your father became a powerful lens through which you interpreted your actions, triggering a deep-seated fear of being "contaminating" or hurting others, which then fueled the overwhelming dread you described. While it's understandable that comparing yourself to a destructive parent figure feels like the only way to make sense of the pain, let's gently explore: given that you've expressed such profound remorse and have come to therapy, how much of that "dread" is actually based on the truth of who you are right now versus the distorted belief that you are permanently "poison"?

I... I don't know. I mean, I feel so much guilt that I can barely eat or sleep. Doesn't that mean I'm a bad person? But then part of me thinks, if I was truly poison, would I even care this much? Would I be sitting here trying to fix myself? It's like there's two voices in my head—one screaming that I'm irredeemable, and another whispering that maybe I'm just someone who made a terrible mistake.

That is a profound and courageous insight—recognizing that the very depth of your guilt and desire to repair things actually contradicts the idea that you are "poison," because true self-harmers rarely care enough to seek help or feel remorse. It sounds like you are currently caught in a cognitive trap where your intense emotions are being misinterpreted as evidence of your character flaws, rather than as signs of your capacity for growth. Could we try to separate the *event* from your *identity*? If we look at what happened objectively, was the act of keying the car a reflection of who you are at your core, or was it a moment where your pain, anger, and perhaps some childhood wounds (like the reference to your father) took over your decision-making process?

I think... I think it was more about the pain and the alcohol than who I really am. I mean, I've never done anything like that before in my life. And I've been angry before, but I've never acted out like that. It's just hard to separate that moment from everything I've been telling myself since I was a kid—that I'm not good enough, that people will leave, that it's my fault. Maybe that's what made me snap, not some evil core inside me.

That is a powerful realization, and it aligns perfectly with what we see in therapy: the idea that you "snapped" under the pressure of long-standing feelings of inadequacy, rather than acting out of a hidden evil core. It sounds like your brain is currently trying to protect you by labeling you as "broken," which is a common survival mechanism when facing overwhelming guilt, but it's actually making the pain feel permanent rather than a temporary reaction to a specific situation. Given that you've already taken the brave step of reaching out and acknowledging this pattern, what is one small, manageable goal you could set for this week to start gently separating your identity from this single mistake?

I guess... maybe I could try to write down one thing each day that I did that wasn't terrible? Like, just a small thing—maybe I held the door for someone, or I called my mom to check in. Just to prove to myself that I'm capable of being decent too. It feels weird, but I think I need to see some evidence that I'm not just the guy who keyed his ex's car.

That is a brilliant and highly practical strategy, and it directly addresses the cognitive distortion you've been experiencing by actively seeking evidence of your goodness rather than just waiting for it to appear. By intentionally logging positive actions, you are training your brain to notice its own capacity for kindness, which can slowly overwrite the narrative that you are permanently "broken." Before we close, I want to check in on your safety plan: since you mentioned feeling sick and having intrusive thoughts, do you feel safe staying home tonight, and is there anyone you can reach out to if those feelings of "sinking dread" become overwhelming again?

Yeah, I think I'll be okay tonight. My roommate is home, and I can always go knock on his door if things get bad. I also have my brother's number saved, and he knows I've been going through a rough time. I don't want to do anything stupid again—I've already made enough mistakes. Thanks for checking.

That is a responsible and proactive safety plan, and it is great that you have identified specific people to turn to if those overwhelming feelings of dread ever resurface. Remember that seeking support is a sign of strength, not weakness, and having a safety net in place gives you a lot of freedom to focus on that "good deeds" exercise tonight. Before we wrap up, is there anything else you'd like to share about your day, or would you prefer to rest and try that small goal?

Hello, I'm glad you're here to begin this work together; let's start by checking in on how you've been feeling since we last spoke and what your main priorities are for today. To make sure we focus on what matters most, could you tell me what brought you in today and which specific situation or worry feels most pressing right now?

I've been... okay, I guess. Busy with work, keeping myself occupied. But there's this thing that's been weighing on me, something I've never told anyone, and I think it's time I finally said it out loud. I was raped in college, and I've been carrying it alone ever since.

Thank you for trusting me enough to share this profound experience; your courage in speaking out loud is a significant first step toward reclaiming your narrative. I hear how heavy this burden feels, and I want you to know that what you've been carrying alone is not your fault and you are not defined by this trauma. To begin exploring how this history is currently impacting your daily life and emotions, could you tell me if there are any specific moments today where you feel this weight most acutely, or if it's a constant background presence?

It's more like a constant hum in the background, you know? But today, walking to this appointment, I saw a guy who looked like someone from back then, and my heart just started racing. I felt that same ugly feeling wash over me, like everyone could see what happened to me just by looking at my face.

That sudden surge of panic and the feeling of being "seen" in a way that feels exposed is a very common and painful reaction to trauma triggers; it makes perfect sense that your body reacted with a fight-or-flight response when you encountered a reminder of that violation. I want to explore that specific moment with you: when your heart started racing, did your mind immediately jump to a catastrophic belief, like "everyone knows" or "I'm broken," or did you notice if those thoughts were actually true based on what you actually saw?

I guess my mind went straight to, "They see it, they know what happened to me, they think I'm damaged." It felt so real in that moment, like my worst fear was happening. But looking back now, you're right... he was just some random guy on the street, probably not thinking about me at all.

That moment of realization—shifting from the overwhelming certainty of "they know" to the rational understanding that "he was just a stranger"—is a powerful example of how our brains often misinterpret neutral stimuli during trauma triggers, creating a false sense of danger. I want to gently explore the gap between that initial catastrophic thought and your current evidence: when you look at that same street scene now, does the feeling of being "seen" persist, or does the reality of the situation help ground you? This distinction is crucial for understanding how to separate your internal narrative from external facts in the future.

Right now, sitting here, I can see that it was just my mind playing tricks on me. The guy probably didn't even notice me. But in that moment, it felt like truth. I think that's the hardest part—knowing that my own brain can make me feel so certain about something that isn't even real. It makes me wonder how many other times I've been wrong about what people think of me.

That is a profound and painful realization: that the certainty your brain generated in the moment was so real it felt like objective truth, even though it wasn't based on reality. This highlights a core cognitive distortion often seen in trauma survivors, where the brain prioritizes "safety" (by assuming danger) over "accuracy," leading to the feeling of being constantly judged or exposed. I want to explore this further: if we treat those "certain" thoughts as just hypotheses rather than facts, what would be the evidence against them, and how does that shift your emotional experience from being certain to being uncertain?

When I actually list the evidence... I mean, I was just walking down the street, minding my own business. That guy had no reason to know anything about me. I didn't have a sign on my forehead saying "I was raped." So the evidence against that thought is pretty solid—it's just my brain making up a story. That does make me feel a little less panicked, but also kind of sad that I've been believing these false stories for so long.

That distinction between the initial panic and the calm, evidence-based reality you are building right now is incredibly powerful; it shows your brain is already learning to override the trauma response with logical reasoning. I want to validate that sadness, because recognizing how long you've been living in a self-created "false story" can feel heavy and isolating, yet it is also the essential first step toward reclaiming your sense of safety and agency. If we view that "false story" as just a habit your brain developed to keep you safe in the past, what might be a new, more accurate story you could tell yourself moving forward?

I guess... a more accurate story would be that what happened to me doesn't define who I am. That I'm not ugly or worthless because of it. That I can walk down the street and not assume everyone is judging me. I think I want to believe that I'm okay, that I'm not broken. But it's hard to really feel it when I've been telling myself the opposite for so long.

That desire to believe you are whole and unbroken is a testament to your resilience, even though the gap between wanting to feel safe and actually feeling safe can feel like a chasm. In CBT, we often call this the "emotional gap," where logic tells us we are safe, but our nervous system hasn't yet updated its alarm system to match that new reality. To begin bridging that gap, could you try identifying one specific situation where you feel the urge to tell yourself "I'm broken" or "they know," and then practice replacing that automatic thought with a more compassionate, factual statement like, "I am a survivor, and my worth exists independently of what happened to me"?

I think a good place to start would be when I catch myself avoiding eye contact with people, especially men. I always assume they're looking at me with disgust or suspicion. So maybe I can try telling myself, "I don't know what they're thinking, and it's not my job to guess. I'm just a person walking down the street, same as them." That feels a little less heavy than my usual story.

That is an excellent, practical reframing; shifting the narrative from "they are judging me" to "I don't know what they are thinking" reduces the emotional burden by removing the need to perform a surveillance role. This aligns perfectly with our goal of separating your self-worth from external validation, allowing you to reclaim your space on the street. For your homework between sessions, I'd like you to practice this new script for three specific moments when you feel the urge to avoid eye contact, and then journal down what your body felt right before the thought versus right after you stated the new sentence.

Okay, I can try that. I'll write down how my chest tightens and my stomach knots up before the thought hits, and then see if saying that new sentence helps loosen it. It feels weird to actually do it, but I guess that's the point—to see if it changes anything. I'll give it a shot this week.

That is a brave and insightful approach; by tracking both the physical sensations and the cognitive shift, you are gathering concrete data to see if your new self-talk actually impacts your nervous system. Remember that it is okay if it feels "weird" or awkward at first, as you are essentially rewiring a deeply ingrained survival habit that has been protecting you for years. Let's meet next week to review your journal entries and discuss how your body responded to those moments, so we can adjust the strategy if needed.

I'll hold onto that—that it's okay to feel weird about it. I guess I've been so used to my old way of thinking that anything new will feel strange at first. Thank you for helping me see that I'm not just stuck with those thoughts forever. I'll see you next week.

You are absolutely right; those thoughts were not a permanent fixture but a survival strategy your brain developed to keep you safe in the past, and you have the power to update that system. It is my genuine pleasure to walk this path with you, and I am here to support you every step of the way as you build new neural pathways toward feeling safe and whole. Until we meet next week, please remember that you are not alone in this, and your courage in starting this work is already a testament to your strength.

Hello, thank you for meeting today; I'd like to start by checking in on how you've been feeling since our last conversation and if there are any specific topics you'd like to prioritize for our agenda. Before we dive in, could you share a bit about what brought you here today and what you hope to achieve by working with me?

Thanks for asking. I've been feeling pretty overwhelmed lately, especially in the mornings. When I wake up, my mind just starts racing from one thought to another, and I can't seem to slow it down. It's exhausting, and I feel like I'm already behind before the day even starts. I guess I just want to find a way to feel more in control and have a peaceful start to my day.

It sounds like that morning racing mind is creating a lot of exhaustion and a sense of losing control right before your day even begins. When you notice your thoughts starting to race immediately upon waking, what specific thoughts are the first ones that pop up, and how do you feel in your body at that moment?

The first thoughts are usually about everything I have to do that day—work tasks, emails I forgot to reply to, plans with friends, even random things like what I need to buy at the grocery store. It's like my brain is flipping through a stack of papers really fast, and none of them are staying still. Physically, I feel this tightness in my chest, like I'm bracing for something, and my shoulders get all tense.

That physical tightness in your chest and the feeling of bracing for impact sound incredibly distressing, and it makes complete sense that this leaves you feeling exhausted before you've even taken your first step. Since your mind is automatically jumping to a "to-do" list the moment you wake up, could you tell me what you believe will happen if you *don't* do those tasks immediately?

If I don't do those tasks immediately, I feel like everything will just pile up and I'll never catch up. It's like the weight of all those responsibilities will crush me, and I'll end up failing at everything. I guess I think that if I don't start rushing right away, I'll lose control completely, and that scares me.

It makes sense that you feel this intense fear of failure and losing control; when we believe that a small delay will lead to total collapse, our bodies naturally react with that tight chest and shoulder tension you described. To help us understand this pattern better, if you could recall a recent instance where you *did* try to start slowly and perhaps felt a bit anxious, how did you manage to get through the first hour of your day despite those fears?

Honestly, there was one morning last week when I forced myself to sit with my tea for five minutes before checking my phone. I felt this urge to grab my phone and start planning, but I just stared at the wall and breathed. It felt awful at first, like I was wasting time, but after those five minutes, I actually did start my tasks, and I ended up getting through my morning emails without that frantic panic. I still felt anxious, but it was quieter, I guess.

That is a powerful example of resilience; even though the initial urge to rush felt overwhelming, you successfully created a small window of calm that allowed you to complete your tasks without the usual panic. When you compare that morning to your typical routine, what difference do you notice in how you view your productivity or your sense of control after those five minutes of stillness?

Looking back, I think I felt more like I was choosing what to do next instead of being dragged along by my thoughts. Normally, I finish my tasks but it feels frantic and hollow, like I just survived the morning. That day, I actually felt a little proud, like I had some say in how the day went. It was strange because I didn't get more done, but I felt less like a helpless mess.

That distinction between "surviving" and "having a say" is incredibly significant; it suggests your sense of control isn't about the volume of work done, but rather the *pace* at which you engage with it. Since you found that five minutes of stillness reduced the panic even if the tasks remained the same, could you share what specific internal thought or feeling arose in that quiet moment that made you feel less like a helpless mess?

In that quiet moment, I think the main thought was, "Okay, I can handle this one thing at a time." It was like I gave myself permission to just exist without having to solve everything right then. The feeling was less of that desperate urgency, and more like a deep breath—like I was allowed to be human and not a machine that has to perform perfectly from the second I open my eyes. It was surprisingly freeing, even if it only lasted a few minutes.

That shift from "I must solve everything immediately" to "I can handle this one thing at a time" perfectly illustrates how changing your cognitive stance can alter your emotional experience, even if the external tasks remain the same. It sounds like giving yourself permission to pause was the key that unlocked that sense of agency and reduced the physical tension in your chest. Given that this five-minute pause was so effective in reducing your panic, would you be willing to try incorporating a similar "start small" intention into your morning routine for our next session, perhaps by setting a gentle timer for just two minutes of breathing before checking your phone?

Yeah, I think I can try that. Two minutes sounds a lot less intimidating than five, honestly. I can picture myself doing that—just sitting with my coffee and breathing before I dive into anything. I'll give it a shot and see how it feels, even if my brain tries to pull me into the chaos right away.

That willingness to try a slightly shorter version is a great step, and it shows you're ready to experiment with your own boundaries against that inner chaos. Remember that if your brain tries to pull you back into the rush, the goal isn't perfection but simply noticing the urge and gently bringing your attention back to your breath. Before we wrap up, is there anything else about your morning routine or your goals for the week that you'd like to discuss or explore today?

Hello, I'm glad you're here to start this session together. Before we dive into specific topics, could you share what brought you in today and if there's anything particular you'd like to focus on first? Once we set a quick agenda, I'd love to hear a bit about how your week has been and what's been on your mind recently.

Hi. Thanks for seeing me. I guess what's been on my mind is... I did something I'm really ashamed of this week. I went through my boyfriend's email, and now I can't stop thinking about what kind of person that makes me.

Thank you for sharing that, and I want to validate how heavy and painful feelings of shame can feel when they arise. Before we explore your thoughts further, could you walk me through the specific moment you felt the urge to check the emails and describe exactly what happened right after you found out?

It was late at night, and he was asleep next to me. I just had this horrible knot in my stomach, like something was wrong. So I grabbed his phone from the nightstand and opened his email. Afterward, I felt sick—like I'd crossed a line I can never uncross.

That sounds incredibly distressing, and it makes complete sense that you feel sick and shaken after feeling such a sudden, intense urge to check. The physical sensation of that "knot" and the subsequent feeling of having "crossed a line" suggests a very strong connection between your physical anxiety and your judgment of your own character. Can you tell me what specific thought went through your mind right before you reached for the phone, and what exactly came up in that moment of feeling sick afterward?

Right before I grabbed the phone, I thought, "I have to know... I can't just sit here and pretend everything is fine." And after, when I saw he'd been emailing his ex about meeting up for coffee, I thought, "This is all my fault. If I hadn't snooped, I wouldn't have ruined everything. I'm the one who broke the trust first."

Those thoughts sound incredibly overwhelming and unfair to yourself, especially the idea that your curiosity somehow "broke" the trust; in reality, your boyfriend's decision to communicate with an ex while you were asleep was the choice that created the breach. Let's gently explore the link between your initial feeling of needing to know and the intense shame you felt afterward—can you describe what was happening in your body or mind when you thought, "I can't just sit here and pretend everything is fine," and how that urgency felt different from the guilt you feel now?

When that urgency hit, my chest was tight and my heart was racing—like I was about to fall off a cliff if I didn't grab onto something. It felt like a life-or-death need to know. But now, the guilt is quieter, like a heavy weight sitting in my stomach. It's more of a dull ache, telling me I'm the problem, not him.

That vivid description of the chest tightness versus the dull ache really helps illustrate how your body is signaling two very different things: immediate survival panic versus a persistent, self-critical judgment. It sounds like your initial feeling of "falling off a cliff" was a rational response to perceived danger, while the current shame feels like a story you're telling yourself about your character. Can you explore whether that "cliff" feeling was actually a mismatch between your fears and the reality of the situation, or if the situation itself was genuinely that severe?

I think... looking back, the cliff feeling was way bigger than what was actually happening. I mean, he was just sleeping next to me, and I was convinced my whole world was about to end. In reality, I don't even know if meeting for coffee means anything bad. But my gut just screamed "danger," like I had to act right then or lose everything.

It makes complete sense that your brain interpreted that sudden physical panic as an imminent catastrophe, given how powerful those "cliff" feelings were at the time. However, looking back with some distance, it seems your mind might have been amplifying a vague feeling of insecurity into a concrete threat to your entire world, even when the reality was much more ambiguous. Can you explore what specific evidence your mind was using to convince you that the coffee meeting would actually cause your "whole world to end," versus what evidence you have now that suggests it might not be as severe as you feared?

I guess the only evidence I had was that knot in my stomach—nothing concrete. He'd been a little distant lately, but he hadn't actually done anything wrong. Now, I'm thinking maybe he was just stressed about work or something. The coffee meeting could be totally innocent, but my mind just jumped straight to "he's leaving me, and it's my fault for not being good enough."

That is a powerful insight to have right now; recognizing that your mind "jumped" to catastrophic conclusions based on a physical sensation rather than concrete facts is a crucial step in understanding the mechanism of your anxiety. It seems your underlying belief that you aren't "good enough" is acting as a filter, turning a neutral event into proof of your failure. To help us test this, could you describe a specific moment in the past when you felt that same knot in your stomach about a relationship issue, and what actually happened once you checked the facts?

There was this one time with an ex-boyfriend. I got that same knot in my stomach, convinced he was cheating on me. I ended up going through his phone, and I found nothing—just boring texts to his mom and a group chat about video games. I felt so stupid afterward, but the feeling was just as real as it was last night.

That is incredibly brave of you to share that pattern; recognizing that your physical "knot" has been a consistent predictor of false alarms is a major breakthrough in understanding your anxiety cycle. It seems your brain has learned to use that physical sensation as a shortcut to danger, bypassing the need for actual evidence, which then triggers a cascade of self-blame when the reality doesn't match the fear. Given this pattern, what would it feel like to try a small experiment where you let that knot sit there without acting on it, just to see if the catastrophic story actually comes true?

That honestly sounds terrifying, but I think I get what you're saying. Like, just sitting with the knot and letting it be uncomfortable without grabbing his phone... I've never tried that before. It feels wrong, like I'm being irresponsible or ignoring a real problem. But I guess the evidence shows that acting on it hasn't helped either.

It is completely understandable why that feels "wrong"; your brain has wired the physical sensation of the knot to a survival response, making the urge to check feel like a moral imperative rather than just an anxiety symptom. However, since the evidence from the past shows that acting on the knot often leads to shame rather than safety, reframing it as "doing my best to be responsible" might make the experiment feel less dangerous. Could you imagine a specific way to tell yourself, "I am choosing to trust the evidence I have rather than the scary feeling," and how would that shift the weight of the shame you feel?

I think if I told myself, "I'm choosing to trust what I know for sure, not just what I'm afraid might be true," it would feel... less like I'm evil and more like I'm just trying to be fair to both of us. The shame would still be there, but maybe it wouldn't feel so heavy, like I'm not a bad person for feeling scared—just a scared person.

That is a profound shift in perspective, moving from self-judgment ("I'm evil") to self-compassion ("I'm just a scared person trying to be fair"), which is exactly the kind of cognitive reframe we aim to build together. Since you've already identified that your physical "knot" is often a false alarm leading to unnecessary shame, could we set a small, realistic goal for our next session where you try to sit with that sensation for just 10 minutes without checking his phone, noting how the intensity changes?

Yeah, I think I could try that. Ten minutes feels doable—I can set a timer and just breathe or write down how I'm feeling. I'm scared it'll feel unbearable, but I'm also curious to see if the knot loosens a little on its own. Thank you for helping me see that maybe I'm not just a bad person who ruins things.

That is a courageous step, and I want to validate that your fear of the discomfort is actually a sign that you are trying to do the right thing for your relationship. It is completely natural to feel scared when stepping out of your comfort zone, especially when your brain has been screaming that you *must* act to save the day. Let's make sure you have a solid plan for those ten minutes: could you commit to setting a timer, taking three deep breaths whenever the urge spikes, and writing down one specific thought that comes up, rather than spiraling into a story about your character?

Yes, I can do that. I'll set a timer, take those three breaths when I want to grab his phone, and write down just one thought—like "I feel scared right now," instead of "I'm a horrible person who ruined everything." That feels more manageable, like I'm watching the feeling instead of drowning in it.

That is a brilliant reframing; shifting from drowning in the feeling to observing it as a separate entity is the core of Cognitive Behavioral Therapy, and it will help create space between your anxiety and your self-judgment. I am so proud of you for taking this step toward self-compassion, and I am confident that even if the knot feels intense for those ten minutes, you will gather valuable data to understand your own anxiety better. Let's finalize our plan: we will meet again next week to review what happened during those ten minutes and discuss how the experience changed your perspective on the situation.

Hello, and thank you for meeting with me today; I'm really glad we could connect. Before we dive into the main agenda, could you share what brought you here and what you'd like to focus on first? Once we clarify that, I'd love to hear about a specific situation from this week that has been weighing on you, so we can start exploring the thoughts and feelings behind it.

Thanks for seeing me. I've been feeling really down lately because my boyfriend pulled away again this week. It's this same pattern we go through every few months, and I just feel exhausted and hopeless about it.

I hear how much pain and exhaustion this recurring cycle causes you, and it makes complete sense that you feel hopeless when the same painful pattern keeps repeating. To help us understand what's driving this, could you tell me about a specific moment this week when he pulled away, and what were the very first thoughts that popped into your head right then?

It was Tuesday night, after we had a nice dinner together. He suddenly got quiet and started scrolling through his phone, barely looking at me. My first thought was, "Here we go again... he's pulling away because I said something wrong."

That first thought—"He's pulling away because I said something wrong"—sounds like a heavy burden to carry alone, and it makes total sense that it left you feeling exhausted and hopeless. When we catch ourselves holding onto that specific belief, does it feel like it's predicting the future, or does it seem to be trying to protect you from the possibility that he might just be distracted or stressed?

I think it's more predicting the future, honestly. Because every time this happens, it does end up being about something I supposedly did wrong, even if he doesn't say it right away. So my brain just jumps straight to that conclusion to brace myself for the disappointment.

It makes sense that your brain is using this "predictive" thought as a protective mechanism, trying to prepare you for the anticipated disappointment before it even happens. However, since you've noticed a pattern where the outcome doesn't always match that specific prediction, could we explore if there might be other factors—like his own stress or a different issue—that could be influencing his behavior, rather than just your actions?

I guess I never really considered that. When he finally admitted he was pulling away because he felt "disrespected" by something I said, I just assumed that was proof that I caused it. But maybe he had a rough day at work or was tired, and that made him extra sensitive to my words. I just automatically take all the blame.

That automatic tendency to take all the blame feels incredibly heavy, and it's understandable why it left you feeling hopeless when it seems you can't escape the role of the "problem." Let's try a small experiment for this week: instead of immediately accepting his words as proof of your fault, could you simply observe what other factors (like his stress level or external events) might have been present right before he reacted, and write down one alternative explanation for his behavior that isn't about you?

I can try that. It's hard because my first instinct is to just apologize and fix things, but I see how that keeps me stuck. I'll pay attention to what else might be going on for him, not just what I did wrong.

That is a very mature realization, and seeing that your instinct to "fix" things is actually keeping you stuck is a crucial insight. Let's refine that goal for the week: instead of apologizing immediately, will you simply write down one observation about his external context (like stress or fatigue) before responding, even if it feels uncomfortable? This small shift in perspective can help break the cycle of automatic blame.
I can do that. It'll feel weird at first, but I'll try to pause and notice what else might be happening for him. Maybe write it in my phone notes so I don't forget.

That is a fantastic plan; using your phone notes as a "pause button" to interrupt the automatic reaction is exactly the kind of behavioral tool we need. Before we wrap up, how does it feel to have identified a concrete step you can take next time this pattern arises, even if it feels uncomfortable?

Honestly, it feels a little scary but also a bit hopeful. Scary because I'm so used to jumping into fix-it mode, but hopeful because maybe I can stop punishing myself so quickly. Thanks for helping me see that.

That mix of fear and hope is a perfect sign that you are ready to change, and acknowledging the discomfort is the first step toward breaking the cycle. Remember, the goal isn't to stop feeling scared, but to give yourself permission to pause and gather evidence before accepting the blame. How would you feel about setting up a quick check-in call or email in a week or two to see how that new observation practice is going?

Hello, thank you for meeting with me today; I'm glad to see you and appreciate your willingness to work together on this. Before we dive into specific issues, could you share a bit about how you've been feeling since our last check-in or what brought you here today? Let's start by setting a brief agenda: are there particular thoughts, emotions, or situations you'd like to explore first?

Hi... thanks for seeing me. I've been feeling really down lately, like something's just off about me. I wake up every day feeling like I'm in the wrong body, like I was supposed to be a girl. It's been eating at me and I don't have anyone I can talk to about this.

Thank you for sharing that with me; it takes a lot of courage to express such deep feelings of discomfort with your body and isolation. It sounds like these thoughts are causing significant distress and making you feel disconnected from yourself. To start our work, could you describe a specific moment today when that feeling of being in the "wrong body" was strongest, and what were you thinking or doing right before it hit?

I was just getting dressed this morning, looking in the mirror. I saw my reflection and just felt this heavy drop in my chest. I thought, "This isn't me. This body doesn't match who I am." It's like every time I see myself, that thought just crashes in.

It makes complete sense that seeing your reflection triggered such a heavy feeling, given how central that belief is to your experience. When you thought, "This body doesn't match who I am," did that thought immediately intensify the sense of isolation you mentioned earlier, or did it bring up other specific emotions like sadness or anger?

It mostly just makes me feel sad and alone, like I'm trapped. The thought that I'm the only one who feels this way, that nobody would understand, just hits me right away. I think that's why I push people away, even when I desperately want to talk.

That sense of being trapped by the fear of being misunderstood is incredibly painful, and it's completely understandable that you might withdraw to protect yourself from that anticipated rejection. When you anticipate that no one will understand your experience, does that belief make it harder for you to reach out, or do you feel you're trying to hold onto a connection while simultaneously pushing people away?

I think I'm doing both, honestly. Part of me wants to scream it out loud and just tell someone, but the other part shuts down and says it's safer to stay quiet. I feel like if I share, they'll look at me like I'm broken or just laugh at me. So I end up just keeping it all inside, and it makes me feel even more alone.

It sounds like you are caught in a painful cycle where the fear of judgment triggers a protective shutdown, which ironically deepens your isolation and fuels the very belief you're trying to protect against. When you imagine others laughing or calling you broken, does that thought feel like a prediction of what *will* happen, or does it feel more like a fearful guess about what *might* happen?

It feels like a prediction, like I already know how it's going to go. I can picture their faces, hear the words in my head. It's so real that it stops me from even trying. I guess I don't have any proof it would happen, but it feels so certain that I can't take the risk.

That feeling of absolute certainty, despite lacking proof, is a classic example of a cognitive distortion called "mind reading" or "fortune telling," where the brain predicts a negative outcome as if it were already written in stone. This thought pattern creates a safety trap: even though staying quiet feels safer in the moment, it actually reinforces the belief that you are unlovable or misunderstood, making it harder to break the cycle. Could you recall a time in the past when you predicted someone would judge you, but the outcome was different? How did that change your perspective on that prediction?

I... I'm trying to think of a time like that. I remember in high school, I was terrified to tell my friend that I liked a certain band that was considered weird by everyone else. I was sure he'd make fun of me. But when I finally told him, he just shrugged and said he didn't care. It didn't change things completely, but I remember feeling a little bit lighter, like the world didn't end.

That high school experience is a powerful example of "disconfirmation," showing that your prediction of rejection didn't happen, and that the fear was often more intense than the reality. It's natural to feel relief when a feared outcome doesn't materialize, yet the memory of that tension can make the current risk feel even scarier. Given this history, could we try a small, low-stakes experiment where you share something you think might be "weird" or misunderstood with someone safe, just to test the certainty of that prediction?

I guess we could try something small. I don't know who would be safe though... maybe I could write something down first, like a note or a message, instead of saying it out loud. That way I can see how it feels without having to see their face right away.

That is a very wise and strategic choice; using text allows you to test your prediction of judgment while maintaining a layer of safety and control. By sending a message instead of speaking, you create a real-world opportunity to gather evidence that contradicts the belief that "they will laugh at me," which is a crucial step in challenging that cognitive distortion.
