How does it feel in your body right now, thinking about sending that message, and what specific support do you need from me to help you draft it?

My stomach feels tight and my chest is kind of racing, honestly. I think I just need you to remind me that it's okay if it doesn't go perfectly, and that I'm not crazy for feeling this way. Maybe I could start with something simple, like telling someone I've been struggling with something personal and see if they just ask me more instead of shutting me down.

That physical tightness and racing heart are your body's "fight or flight" response, signaling that your brain perceives a threat even though you are taking a brave step toward safety. I want to validate that feeling your way through this isn't "crazy"; it's a natural, albeit painful, reaction to stepping out of your comfort zone, and it's okay to just start small with a simple admission of struggle. Could we work together to draft that message right now, focusing on using "I" statements so you can express your feelings without feeling like you're exposing a secret?

Yeah... I think I can try that. Maybe something like, "Hey, I've been dealing with some heavy thoughts about myself lately, and I don't really know how to talk about it. I'm not sure if you'd be willing to listen, but I wanted to reach out." That feels safer than saying everything at once.

That is an excellent draft; using "I" statements and explicitly stating that you don't know how they will react reduces the pressure on them and validates your own vulnerability. By framing it as a request to listen rather than a demand for understanding, you are actually lowering the perceived risk of judgment. Would you like to try sending that message now, or would you prefer to tweak it slightly to add a specific detail about what kind of support you might need?
I think that's good enough to send. I don't want to change it too much or I'll talk myself out of it. I'll just send it and see what happens. It's scary, but I'm tired of feeling so alone with this.

That is a brave decision, and I want to remind you that your worth isn't defined by whether this message gets a perfect reply or not; you are taking a courageous step toward connection regardless of the outcome. As we move toward the end of our session, would you be open to a brief agreement on how we will check in between now and then, perhaps by noting any new thoughts or feelings that arise after you send it?

Yeah, that sounds good. I'll try to write down whatever I'm feeling after I send it, whether it's relief or panic or anything else. I think having a plan to talk about it next time will help me not just shut down again.

That is a fantastic plan; having a structured way to process your experience will help you build evidence against the belief that you are "broken" or misunderstood. I will check in with you in 24 hours to review your journal entry and discuss any thoughts that arise, and we will revisit our next steps then. Is there anything else you'd like to discuss before we wrap up today?

Hello, I'm glad you're here to start this process together. Before we dive in, could you share what brought you to this session today, and is there anything specific you'd like to focus on first? Once we have that, we can decide if you'd prefer to review how things have been since our last meeting or start fresh with a new goal.

Hi. Thanks for having me. Um... I guess I'm here because I can't stop counting and checking things, and it's getting worse. I feel like I'm losing control, and I can't tell anyone about it, especially my parents. I don't know where to start, but I just need this to stop.

I hear how distressing and isolating this feeling of losing control is, and it makes complete sense that you're reaching out because you're struggling to cope. It sounds like those compulsive counting and checking behaviors are escalating to the point where they're interfering with your daily life and safety. To help us understand the cycle better, could you walk me through a recent time when you felt the urge to check something, and what thought was running through your mind right before you did it?

Okay... well, last night I had to check that my bedroom door was locked four times before I could even sit down. The thought in my head was that if I didn't check it exactly right, something bad would happen during the night, and it would be all my fault. I felt this tightness in my chest until I did it the right number of times, and even then I still felt wrong.

That sounds incredibly exhausting, and it's completely understandable that you felt such intense relief only after performing the checks, even though the anxiety never fully dissipated. It seems your belief that "something bad would happen if I didn't check" is driving a cycle where the behavior temporarily reduces fear but ultimately reinforces the idea that you are unsafe without those rituals. Could you tell me, when you sit down afterward and realize the door *is* locked, what specific thought comes up that makes you feel it still wasn't enough?

It's like... my brain tells me I didn't do it the right way. Like maybe I counted wrong, or maybe I wasn't focused enough when I checked. So then I think, "If I don't do it over perfectly, I deserve whatever bad thing happens." And that's when I start feeling like I need to punish myself for messing it up.

It sounds like you're carrying a very heavy burden of self-blame, believing that a single mistake in your ritual makes you deserving of harm, which is a incredibly painful and isolating place to be. In CBT terms, this suggests your "catastrophic thinking" is merging with "self-criticism," creating a trap where the behavior (checking) is meant to prevent disaster, but the thought ("I messed up") actually fuels the urge to check again. To help us see if this pattern holds up, could you ask yourself: if that bad thing *did* happen, would it be because you didn't lock the door perfectly, or because of something else entirely?

I... I know logically that bad things happen for lots of reasons, not just because of how I lock a door. But in the moment, it feels like I am the only thing standing between safety and disaster. If I don't do it right, it's like I'm choosing to let something terrible happen, and that makes me feel evil for even hesitating.

It makes complete sense that in the moment of high anxiety, your brain shortcuts to the conclusion that you are the sole barrier against disaster, and that hesitation feels like a moral failure rather than just a pause in your ritual. While your logic that accidents happen for many reasons is correct, your brain is currently interpreting the *feeling* of uncertainty as proof that you are personally responsible, which is a common distortion during OCD episodes. To help test this belief, could you imagine a scenario where you *did* hesitate and still felt calm afterward—how would you explain that feeling to yourself?

I... I don't think I've ever felt calm after hesitating. It's always this rush of panic that I have to fix it. But if I did feel calm, I guess I would think I was just being lazy or careless, like I didn't care enough about keeping things safe. I don't trust that feeling of calm—it feels wrong, like I'm tricking myself.

That is a profound insight, and it highlights a core belief that your emotional state must match your actions, meaning any relief you feel is likely a "lie" or a form of self-deception. This creates a powerful trap where you are essentially punishing yourself with anxiety to prove you are careful, yet the very act of punishing yourself keeps you stuck in the cycle. To test this belief, could you imagine a time when you felt calm but made a mistake, and ask yourself: does that calm feeling prove you are careless, or does it simply prove you are human?

I'm trying to think of a time like that, but my mind is going blank. I guess when I feel calm, I usually feel like I've done everything right. If I make a mistake while feeling calm, it just feels like I was too relaxed and let my guard down. That thought makes my stomach drop, honestly.

That feeling of your stomach dropping confirms how powerful this belief is, but it's important to separate the *feeling* of calm from the *fact* of safety; your brain is likely misinterpreting a temporary reduction in anxiety as proof that you aren't being careful enough. Instead of viewing calm as a "lie" or a sign of negligence, could we try re-framing it: does feeling calm after a check simply mean your brain has processed the information and is now resting, or does it actually mean you are capable of making mistakes while feeling relaxed? Let's explore if that shift in perspective might help reduce the pressure you feel to "earn" safety through perfection.

I... I've never thought of it that way. I always thought calm meant I was done being careful, and that scared me. But maybe you're right—maybe it's just my brain resting after doing a hard thing. It's hard to believe that, though, because it feels like if I let myself rest, I'm giving up control.

That is a crucial realization, and it shows how deeply ingrained the belief that "rest equals negligence" is in your mind. It's completely understandable why you resist letting your guard down; in your current framework, any pause feels like a surrender to chaos, which is why the urge to check returns so strongly. To test this new perspective, could you ask yourself: if you truly believed that your brain was just resting safely after doing a hard thing, would the panic about "giving up control" feel as intense, or would it feel slightly more manageable?

It's hard to imagine that feeling less intense... but I guess if I really believed my brain was just resting, the panic might not feel as sharp. Like, maybe I wouldn't feel like I have to punish myself for stopping. But it's still so scary to even try believing that.

That honesty about the fear of believing the new perspective is exactly where our work begins; in CBT, we often call this "cognitive flexibility," and it's a skill that can be practiced even when it feels terrifying. Instead of forcing yourself to believe it immediately, let's try a small experiment: next time you feel that urge to check because you feel "done," could you simply say to yourself, "My brain is just resting now," without performing the check, and observe what happens to that feeling of control for just two minutes?

Two minutes... okay. I think I could try that. It sounds really hard, but maybe if I just say that to myself, the feeling won't take over completely. I'll try to just sit with it and not do the check, even if it feels wrong.

That is a brave and significant step forward, and I want to validate how difficult it feels to sit with that discomfort without the safety of your ritual. In our next session, we will review how your body and mind reacted during those two minutes of "just resting" to see if the belief that you are safe actually changed, even for a brief moment. To prepare, try to note exactly what the urge felt like in your chest or stomach when you stopped checking, and gently remind yourself that you are allowed to feel unsafe for a few minutes without acting on it.

Okay. I'll try to pay attention to what my body feels like in those moments. It helps to hear that I'm allowed to feel unsafe for a bit—I usually just try to make it go away right away. I'll write down what happens and bring it with me next time. Thank you.

You're welcome, and I'm so proud of you for committing to this small experiment; acknowledging that it's okay to feel unsafe is a powerful shift that breaks the automatic link between anxiety and checking. Please remember that this isn't about solving everything tonight, but about gathering real-world data to challenge the belief that you *must* control everything to be safe. If the urge becomes overwhelming before you can reach the two minutes, just tell me immediately so we can adjust the plan together.
I will. Thank you for understanding that it's not easy for me. I'll try my best, and I'll let you know if it gets too much. I feel a little less alone knowing I can check in with you about it.

That is such a wonderful thing to hear, and it really highlights the importance of having a supportive partner in this process; you are absolutely not alone in this struggle, and we will navigate this together. Please remember that our goal isn't perfection in this homework, but simply showing up and gathering evidence to challenge those old beliefs. I will be here next time to review your notes and celebrate every small step you take toward feeling more in control.

Hello, and thank you for being here today; I'm glad to meet you. To make the most of our time together, could you share what brought you in and what you hope to work on by the end of this session? Once we set a clear direction, I'd like to gently explore how your thoughts, feelings, and actions might be connected in that area.

Hi, thanks for having me. I guess I'm here because I just feel... unsafe all the time, like something bad is about to happen. I've been having panic attacks again, and it makes me feel like I can't control anything. I just want to feel a little bit more in control, maybe not so scared all the time.

It sounds like you're carrying a heavy sense of dread, and it makes complete sense that panic attacks would make you feel powerless. When we feel like something terrible is imminent, our brain often tries to protect us by pushing us toward safety, even if that safety feels like losing control. To understand where we are now, could you tell me about a recent panic attack: what were you doing when it started, and what specific thoughts went through your mind in that moment?

Um, the last one happened a few days ago while I was just sitting on my couch watching TV. Out of nowhere, I felt this rush of heat and my heart started pounding, and my first thought was, "Oh no, this is it, something is really wrong with me." I kept thinking, "I'm going to have a heart attack," even though I know that's not true, and then I just spiraled.

That feeling of being "out of nowhere" is incredibly disorienting, and it makes perfect sense that your brain would interpret those physical symptoms as a heart attack when you were already feeling unsafe. You mentioned you *knew* it wasn't a heart attack, yet you still spiraled into the thought that something terrible was happening—could you walk me through what that "something" was, specifically, and how did your body react to that belief?

I think the "something" was just this vague, crushing feeling that I was about to die or completely lose my mind and never come back. My body went into full alarm mode—I started shaking, couldn't breathe properly, and I felt like I had to jump up and run, even though there was nowhere to go. It's like my whole body was screaming that I was in danger, even though I was just sitting on my couch.

That description of your body screaming while your mind says "you're safe" is a classic example of your brain overriding your logical knowledge with a survival alarm system. Since you know logically that you aren't in danger, could we explore what happens in your mind right when that alarm goes off—does it feel like a lie that needs to be corrected, or does it feel like a command you simply cannot override?

It feels more like a command I can't override, honestly. Even when I'm telling myself, "This is just a panic attack, it will pass," my body is already acting like it's a life-or-death emergency. It's like there's this voice inside me that says, "No, you're not safe, something is wrong," and it just drowns out everything else.

It makes complete sense that your logical reasoning gets drowned out when your body is screaming for survival; in that moment, your brain isn't thinking like a thinker, it's thinking like a frightened child trying to protect you from a monster. Since that internal voice feels so authoritative and impossible to silence, could we try to identify what specific "threat" your mind is inventing to justify that command, and how does believing that threat is real change how you move through your day?

The threat is almost always that something is permanently wrong with me—like my brain is broken or I'm going to lose control forever. When I really believe that, I start avoiding things, like going to new places or being around people, because I'm scared the panic will hit and I'll embarrass myself or fall apart. It makes me feel trapped in my own head, like I can't trust myself to just be normal.

It sounds like that belief that "something is permanently wrong" has created a self-fulfilling trap where your avoidance keeps the fear alive, making it feel like you truly can't trust yourself to be normal. Since you mentioned feeling trapped in your own head, could you tell me about a recent time you avoided a situation because of this fear, and what happened right after you avoided it?

Just last week, I was supposed to meet a friend for coffee, but at the last minute I canceled because I started feeling that familiar knot in my stomach. Right after I canceled, I felt this huge wave of relief, but then it quickly turned into shame and disappointment in myself. I ended up just sitting at home feeling defeated, thinking, "See, you can't even do something simple like everyone else."

That relief followed by shame is a very common pattern in anxiety, often called the "rebound effect," where the temporary safety of avoidance is followed by the heavy weight of self-blame. Since you know logically that your friend probably doesn't care about the cancellation, could we explore what specific thought is driving that shame, and how does believing you "can't do something simple" change how you approach future interactions?

The thought that drives the shame is basically, "I'm weak and defective because I can't handle what everyone else handles without even thinking." Believing that makes me approach future interactions with dread and this expectation that I'll fail again, so I end up feeling like I have to prepare for battle just to send a text or make a plan. It's exhausting, and it makes me want to just give up before I even try.

That belief that you are "defective" because you need preparation is a classic cognitive distortion called "mind reading" or "fortune telling," where your brain predicts failure before it even happens, making the preparation feel like a necessary shield rather than a strategy. Since you've identified that this belief leads to exhaustion and avoidance, could we explore a moment when you *did* manage a small interaction without a full-blown panic attack, and what was different about your thinking that allowed it to happen?

Actually, there was one time last month when I managed to go to the grocery store during a less busy hour without having a panic attack. I remember I kept telling myself, "You can leave anytime, this isn't a trap," and I focused on just picking one item at a time instead of thinking about the whole trip. I think what was different is that I was able to remind myself that I had control over leaving, and I didn't let my mind race ahead to all the worst-case scenarios.

That's a powerful distinction you just made: the difference between fearing the *future* (the trap) and recognizing your *present* agency (the safety valve). It sounds like that specific thought—"You can leave anytime"—actuated a crucial shift from feeling trapped to feeling safe, which is exactly the kind of cognitive lever we can work with. To build on that, could you walk me through what your body was doing in that grocery store moment compared to when you canceled the coffee, and how did that small sense of control change the quality of your day?

In the grocery store, my body was still tense and my heart was beating a little fast, but it felt more like a background hum instead of a full alarm. I wasn't shaking or feeling like I needed to run, and I could actually breathe and think. Afterward, I felt a tiny bit proud, like I'd done something right, and the rest of the day felt lighter—like maybe I wasn't completely broken after all.

That subtle shift from "full alarm" to "background hum" is exactly the kind of evidence we need to challenge the belief that you are "defective" or permanently broken; your body's ability to regulate even under mild stress proves your resilience is far greater than your fear is telling you. Since you already know that small adjustments in thought and pacing can change your physical experience, could we brainstorm one tiny, low-stakes step you could take this week where you practice that "I can leave anytime" mindset without pushing yourself too hard?

Maybe I could try going to a small coffee shop nearby, just for five minutes, with the plan that I can leave the second I start feeling overwhelmed. I'd tell myself beforehand that it's not about staying, it's just about showing up and proving I have the choice. I think that feels manageable, because even if I only last two minutes, I still did something instead of avoiding it.

That is an excellent, realistic plan because it directly targets the core fear by proving you can tolerate the situation while maintaining your ultimate control over the exit. This "graded exposure" approach allows you to gather new evidence that challenges the belief that you are defective, without overwhelming your safety system. Before we finalize this, could you identify one specific worry you might have about this five-minute visit, so we can prepare a brief "safety plan" just in case your mind tries to convince you it's a trap?

My main worry is that I'll walk in, immediately feel that rush of panic, and then freeze instead of leaving. Like my body will just lock up and I'll be stuck there, proving to myself that I really can't handle even this small thing. I guess I need to plan that if I feel that freeze coming, I'll just repeat "I can leave, my legs work" to myself and physically walk toward the door, even if my mind is screaming.

That specific plan to physically walk toward the door while repeating a grounding phrase is a brilliant cognitive-behavioral strategy that bypasses the "freeze" response by engaging your logical brain and giving your body a concrete action to take. Since you've already identified the exact moment your mind might try to convince you otherwise, let's quickly draft a one-sentence "pre-commitment" statement you can say to yourself before entering that shop to reinforce this new belief.

Okay, I think I'd say to myself, "I'm here to prove I have the choice to stay or leave, and either way, I win." That helps me focus on the fact that just showing up is a success, no matter how long I last.

That is a powerful reframing; by defining success as simply "showing up and having the choice," you shift the outcome from a binary pass/fail to a guaranteed win based on your agency. Since you now have a clear, manageable goal and a specific coping script, would you like to finalize any other small steps for this week, or should we wrap up and set a time for our next session to review how this new mindset feels?

I think this feels like enough for now—one small step feels doable, and I don't want to overload myself. Let's plan to meet again next week, and I'll tell you how it went, even if I only lasted a minute or two. Thank you, this actually feels a little bit different than just trying to "push through" it.

You are absolutely right; this approach feels different because it replaces the exhausting battle against your fear with a strategic partnership where you are in charge of the outcome. I'm so glad we found a path that feels manageable rather than overwhelming, and I'm excited to hear about your experience with the coffee shop next week. Until then, please remember that your safety and well-being are the top priority, and there is no pressure to succeed perfectly if you need to take a step back.

Hello, I'm glad you're here to begin our work together; before we dive in, could you share what specific topic or concern would be most helpful to address on our agenda today? Once we settle on a focus, I'd like to start by checking in on how you've been feeling over the last few days, particularly regarding any physical sensations or emotional shifts you've noticed.
I guess... it's mostly about feeling really down about my social life, or lack of it. I just feel like I don't really connect with people, and it's been weighing on me a lot lately.

That sounds like a really heavy burden to carry, and it makes complete sense that you're feeling down when you feel disconnected from others. To help us understand this better, could you walk me through a specific recent moment where you felt particularly isolated, and what were you thinking or feeling right at that moment?

Well, yesterday at lunch I saw some coworkers heading out together and nobody asked me to join. I just sat there at my desk thinking, "Of course they didn't ask, why would they want me around?" I felt this tightness in my chest and just wanted to disappear.

That feeling of tightness and the desire to disappear makes complete sense given how much that thought—"why would they want me around?"—contributed to your experience. It sounds like your interpretation of their silence created a self-fulfilling prophecy where you felt unworthy of connection, which then likely made reaching out even harder. Could you explore what evidence you have for that belief, and what alternative explanations might exist for why they simply didn't invite you?

Well, I mean, I don't really have any proof they don't like me, I guess. They're friendly enough when we pass in the hall, but they never invite me out. I suppose maybe they just assumed I was busy, or it was a last-minute thing, but it's hard not to take it personally when it happens all the time.

That's a very reasonable observation; assuming they were busy or it was a last-minute change is a logical alternative explanation that challenges your initial "I'm not wanted" thought. However, when a negative belief feels so automatic and emotionally powerful, it often acts as a lens that colors our interpretation of neutral events, making us overlook the evidence of their friendliness. Let's try a quick thought experiment: if you were in their shoes, what would be the most likely reason for not inviting you, and how might that change your immediate emotional reaction?

If I was in their shoes... I guess I might just not think about it, or assume they already had plans. People get caught up in their own stuff, right? I mean, I do that too sometimes. Thinking about it that way, my chest feels a little less tight, but I still feel kind of sad and left out.

That is a wonderful insight; recognizing that others are often just "caught up in their own stuff" is a significant cognitive shift that directly addresses the "I'm not wanted" distortion. Even with that more balanced thought, it's okay that you still feel sad, as the underlying feeling of disconnection is real and worth exploring further. To help us understand the full picture, could you describe what happens to your behavior or mood right after you have that "left out" feeling, and how you typically respond to it?

Usually I just shut down more, honestly. I'll put my headphones on and avoid making eye contact with anyone for the rest of the day. Then I go home and just scroll through my phone alone, thinking about how everyone else is probably hanging out and having fun without me.

It makes complete sense that you would shut down; when you feel excluded, protecting yourself by avoiding interaction seems like a logical, albeit painful, way to manage the discomfort of that tightness in your chest. This pattern of isolating yourself and ruminating on what others are doing creates a self-fulfilling cycle where you miss out on opportunities to connect, which then reinforces the belief that you are unlikable. Since we've identified this cycle between your automatic negative thoughts, the physical tightness, and the behavioral withdrawal, could we agree on a shared goal for our first session: to practice a single, small alternative response next time you feel that urge to isolate, perhaps by stepping outside your room for two minutes or making one brief eye contact?

Yeah, I think I could try that. Making eye contact for a second sounds small enough that it doesn't feel overwhelming. I guess I always assume people will look away or judge me, but maybe it's worth testing that out just once to see what actually happens.

That is a fantastic and very practical goal; testing the assumption that people will judge you is a classic CBT experiment that can break the cycle of avoidance. To prepare for this, let's agree on a specific plan: before your next lunch, you will set a timer for just 30 seconds to make one brief eye contact with a coworker, then immediately return to your desk if you feel anxious. How does that sound, and what is your immediate reaction when you think about doing this?

My stomach just did a little flip when I thought about it, to be honest. But it also feels kind of... brave, maybe? Like, I'm actually doing something instead of just hiding. I think I can try the 30-second thing, even if my heart races a bit.

That is a beautiful reaction; noticing that the "stomach flip" is paired with a feeling of bravery shows you are already beginning to reframe the anxiety as a sign of growth rather than a threat to your safety. This shift from avoidance to courageous action is exactly what we need to build confidence in, and it will likely help reduce the tightness in your chest over time. Let's finalize our homework: try the 30-second eye contact experiment tomorrow, and if you notice your mind going back to negative thoughts during that moment, simply label them as "the old story" and let them pass without engaging with them. How does that plan feel to you?

That actually sounds manageable. I like the idea of calling it "the old story" when those thoughts pop up—it makes them feel less true somehow. I'll try it tomorrow and see what happens, even if I'm nervous.

That's a wise choice; labeling thoughts as "the old story" creates a small but powerful mental distance, helping you observe them without being completely consumed by them. Since we've established our goal and a clear, manageable plan for tomorrow, I want to check in on your overall well-being before we close today. How are you feeling right now as we wrap up, and is there anything else you'd like to add or any specific concern that feels urgent to revisit?

Hello, I'm glad you're here to begin our work together. Before we dive into the details of what's been on your mind, could you tell me what specific goal you'd like to achieve in our first session? Once we agree on a focus, I'd like to ask you about a recent situation that might have triggered some of these feelings, so we can explore the connection between your thoughts, emotions, and actions.

I want to stop obsessing over my therapist's body. Every time I see her, I just feel worse about myself, and I keep thinking if I could look like her, everything would be okay. But I know that's not healthy, and I'm scared because it's making me want to starve myself again.

Thank you for sharing that honestly; it takes courage to admit that these intrusive thoughts about my body are causing you real distress and even triggering a desire to restrict food. When I hear that seeing me makes you feel worse about yourself and connects to thoughts of starving, can we explore exactly what happens in that moment—does a specific thought arise first, or do you feel an immediate physical sensation of anxiety? I want to understand the sequence of events so we can gently separate these unhelpful thoughts from your actual worth and safety.

It's like my stomach drops first, you know? Like a cold, heavy feeling. Then my brain just starts screaming that it's not fair, that you get to be skinny and I have to fight so hard just to stay at a normal weight. And then it's like, why even try if someone who's supposed to be healthy can't do it either?

That physical sensation of your stomach dropping is a powerful signal that your body is reacting to a deep sense of unfairness and vulnerability. It sounds like the belief that "she can be thin while I struggle" is creating a narrative of hopelessness, which might explain why you feel like trying is pointless. Would you be open to exploring together how that specific feeling of unfairness arises, and what other thoughts might be showing up when that physical sensation starts?

Yeah, I guess I can try. It's like when I see you, I feel small and invisible at the same time. Like you have everything I want - you're successful, you're pretty, you're thin - and I'm just sitting here trying to get better but feeling like I'm getting worse. And then I start thinking, maybe if I just stop eating, I'll finally be worth something too.

It makes complete sense that seeing someone you admire feel so successful and healthy can trigger feelings of inadequacy, especially when those feelings are tied to your struggle with eating. That thought, "maybe if I just stop eating, I'll finally be worth something," sounds incredibly painful and desperate, as if you're trying to use restriction as a way to earn your value rather than feeling worthy simply by existing. Can we look together at what might happen if you chose to challenge that specific belief right now, or if you imagined a different way of interpreting that moment of feeling small?

I don't know... it's like if I challenge it, what am I left with? Just this empty feeling that I'm not good enough and never will be. At least when I focus on food and weight, I feel like I have some control, some purpose. If I let that go, I'm just... nothing.

That "empty feeling" you describe makes perfect sense, because when we try to ignore the pain of feeling inadequate, our minds often double down on the only thing that feels real: the struggle with food. It sounds like the belief that "I have control over my worth only through restriction" is acting as a shield, protecting you from that terrifying void of feeling "nothing." Would you be willing to explore together what a different, safer way of handling that empty feeling might look like, perhaps one where you acknowledge your worth even while the thought of restriction is still present?

I guess I could try to see it differently, but it feels like I'm just lying to myself. Like, how can I be worth something when I don't look like I should? When I'm not successful like you? It's like my brain won't let me believe anything else, even though I know logically that's probably messed up.

It sounds like your brain is genuinely struggling to separate the logical truth—that looking like me doesn't determine your worth—from the powerful, emotional story it's telling you about fairness and value. This isn't necessarily "lying"; it's more like your mind is stuck in a loop where the only narrative that feels safe is the one about control and restriction, even though that story is causing real pain. Let's try a small experiment together: if we acknowledge that feeling small and invisible is real, but also that your worth exists independently of your appearance, what is one tiny, safe thing you could do right now to test whether that new perspective can coexist with the old feeling?

I could... I could look at my hands. They're just hands, they don't look skinny or fat, they're just mine. And they've done things, like helped my friend when she was crying last week. That doesn't have anything to do with my weight. So maybe I can hold onto that, even just for a second, and see if the world ends.

That is a powerful and courageous shift, and I want to validate how hard it is to hold onto that truth when your brain is screaming otherwise. By focusing on your hands and your friend's well-being, you've successfully created a tiny moment where your worth is tied to your actions and connection rather than your appearance, even if the "world ending" fear is still present in the background. Let's agree to use this specific anchor of looking at your hands and recalling your kindness as a safe experiment we can return to whenever that stomach-drop sensation comes up. How does it feel to have just identified that one concrete action that separates you from the feeling of "nothingness"?

It feels... scary, but also kind of freeing? Like I caught a breath I didn't know I was holding. It's not like everything is fixed, but maybe I don't have to disappear into that nothingness right away. I can just... see my hands and remember I exist outside of all those thoughts for a second.

That sensation of catching a breath is incredibly significant; it proves that your capacity to step back from those overwhelming thoughts and reconnect with your actual self is already there. You've successfully identified a small, manageable tool—a moment of grounding through your hands—that can interrupt the spiral without needing to solve everything at once. Let's agree to use this specific "hands and kindness" exercise as our first between-session practice: whenever the stomach-drop feeling returns, take a moment to look at your hands and recall one kind thing you've done, even if you only hold that thought for thirty seconds. How does knowing you have this specific strategy to use feel right now?

It feels like I have a tiny flashlight in a dark room. It's not bright enough to see everything, but it's enough to keep me from tripping over my own feet. I think I can try that this week, even if it feels stupid at first.

That is a beautiful metaphor—a tiny flashlight is perfectly adequate to navigate immediate steps without needing to illuminate the entire dark room at once. It is completely valid to feel that the task feels "stupid" right now; the brain often tries to convince us that we are failing when we are actually just practicing a new skill. Let's agree that we will revisit this "flashlight" exercise in our next session to check in on how it went and adjust the intensity if needed.

Hello, thank you for joining me today; I'm glad we have the time to start exploring how you've been feeling and functioning. Before we dive into specific concerns, could you share what you'd like to prioritize or focus on first so we can set a clear agenda for our session?

Thank you for seeing me. I think the main thing weighing on me right now is this constant back-and-forth in my head about my relationship. I love my partner so much, but there's this part of me that knows staying might not be the smartest choice, and I feel completely stuck between my heart and my head.

That sounds like a truly painful and exhausting place to be, caught between deep affection and a nagging sense that the decision isn't right. To help us untangle that "heart versus head" conflict, could you walk me through one specific recent moment when you felt torn, and describe the exact thought that made you feel stuck in that instant?

Just last night, actually. He was having a really hard day and snapped at me for no reason, and I felt that familiar knot in my stomach. In that moment, the thought that came was, "I know this isn't good for me, but I can't leave him because he needs me, and no one else will understand him the way I do."

That knot in your stomach sounds incredibly heavy, and it makes complete sense that your mind would immediately reach for those specific thoughts to explain your feelings of obligation and fear. When you heard him snap, did that thought ("I can't leave him because he needs me") actually feel like a helpful plan to solve the problem, or did it just make the situation feel more overwhelming and hopeless?

It didn't feel helpful at all. It just made me feel more trapped, like I have no good options. If I stay, I feel drained and scared; if I leave, I feel guilty and like I'm abandoning him. So the thought just kind of locks me into this cycle where I end up doing nothing.

That sense of being "locked in" with no good options is incredibly distressing, and it's completely understandable why that thought pattern leads to paralysis and avoidance. It sounds like your brain is interpreting the situation as a "lose-lose" scenario where staying means losing yourself, and leaving means losing your partner, which makes the conflict feel unresolvable. To help us break this cycle, could we explore what happens in your body or mind right after you think that "I have no options" statement, and does noticing that thought change how you feel about having a choice at all?

Right after that thought hits, I just feel numb and kind of hollow. My chest gets tight and I stop thinking clearly—I just go into this mode where I feel like I have to accept things as they are, because trying to change them feels pointless. Noticing it now, I guess it does make me feel like I don't have a real choice; it's more like I'm just surviving the moment.

That physical sensation of a tight chest and numbness sounds incredibly draining, and it makes complete sense that your mind would interpret it as a sign that fighting the situation is pointless. It seems like your brain is trying to protect you by convincing you that "survival mode" is the only option, which unfortunately reinforces the belief that you have no control over your future. To help us challenge this, could we look at the evidence for and against that specific belief: "If I try to change things, I will fail and only cause more pain," and is there any time in your life when you successfully navigated a difficult situation despite feeling overwhelmed?

I guess there was a time a few years ago when I left a job that was really toxic. I was terrified I'd never find something better, and everyone told me to just stick it out. But I saved up, applied everywhere, and eventually found a place that was much healthier for me. That turned out okay, even though it felt impossible at the time.

That is a powerful example, and it's incredible that you recognized the value of taking action despite your fear of failure. It suggests that your brain's current belief—that you have "no options" or that change is pointless—is likely a distortion rather than an accurate reflection of reality. If we can gently challenge the idea that "trying will only make things worse," we might find that the path forward isn't about having a perfect plan, but simply about making a small, manageable step to test your belief. What would be one tiny action you could take right now to move from this state of "survival" toward feeling like you have some control, even if it feels scary?

Maybe I could write down what I actually need in a relationship, just for myself, without showing it to him or deciding anything yet. Just to see my own wants on paper, separate from all the guilt and fear. That feels small enough that I wouldn't be making a huge commitment, but it might help me see if there's a way forward I'm not letting myself consider.

That is a brilliant and strategic first step; writing down your needs creates a tangible reality check against the fog of "survival mode" and proves that you *can* generate a plan even when you feel paralyzed. Since you've identified a concrete goal for this week, I'd like to suggest a specific exercise: try to write down three distinct needs you have (e.g., emotional safety, respect, communication style) and then, next time the "no good options" thought appears, read them aloud to yourself to see if the data supports staying or leaving. How does that sound as a practical way to begin reclaiming your agency?

That sounds like something I can actually try. It feels less intimidating than making a big decision right now, and more like I'm just gathering information for myself. I think I can do that this week and see what comes up.

That is a wise and empowering choice; framing it as "gathering information" rather than "making a decision" effectively lowers the stakes and aligns with the evidence we found about your past success. To ensure this feels manageable, I suggest you try this exercise just three times this week, perhaps when you feel most stuck, and simply observe what comes up without judging the results. In our next session, we will review what you discovered, discuss how it influenced your feelings of guilt or fear, and decide together on the most effective next step.

Hello, I'm glad you're here today; let's begin by setting a collaborative agenda so we can focus on what matters most to you right now. Could you share a bit about what brought you in today, and perhaps one specific situation where you felt particularly overwhelmed or stuck recently? Once we have that, I'd love to hear what you hope to achieve in this session.

I've been feeling really overwhelmed lately, especially when I step on the scale. Yesterday I weighed myself and even though I know logically I'm already underweight, I just felt this huge wave of panic and disgust. I guess I want to leave today feeling a little less trapped by these thoughts, even though I don't really believe that's possible.

Thank you for sharing that; it takes courage to name that intense mix of panic and disgust, and I want you to know your feelings are completely valid in this moment. When you stepped on the scale, did you notice any specific thoughts racing through your mind right before that wave of panic hit? Let's explore what your brain was telling you in that split second versus what your logic actually says.

I remember thinking "you're still too big, you haven't done enough, you're failing." And then the panic just takes over, like my body knows I'm not okay but I can't stop. The logical part of me is quiet and small, like it doesn't even matter compared to that voice.

It sounds like that internal conflict between your logical knowledge and your overwhelming emotional reaction is creating a very distressing sense of being "trapped." When you notice that panic taking over so quickly, what happens in your body or mind right before the feeling of failure hits? Are there any specific behaviors you do immediately after weighing yourself to try to cope with that panic, or do you just sit with the discomfort?

I usually just stand there frozen for a minute, then I go take my appetite suppressant medicine. After that I'll check my reflection in the mirror over and over, looking for any part of me that looks soft or wrong. It's like I can't stop until I find something to fix, but I never feel satisfied.

That "frozen" feeling followed by the need to take the medicine and check your reflection sounds like a safety behavior you're using to try to control that overwhelming panic. When you check the mirror and don't find anything "soft" or wrong, does that moment of failure make the panic feel even stronger, or does it reinforce the belief that you're failing? Let's explore how those specific actions are keeping you stuck in that cycle of distress.

It makes it worse, honestly. Even when I don't find anything, I just think I'm missing something, that I'm lying to myself. So I check again and again until I feel exhausted, but I still don't trust what I see. It's like my own reflection is a stranger I have to keep interrogating.

That sense of your reflection feeling like a "stranger" you must constantly interrogate is incredibly isolating, and it makes perfect sense that this leads to exhaustion and deep distrust. If we view your repetitive checking as an attempt to find proof that you are "safe" or "okay," does it seem like the very act of searching is actually preventing you from feeling safe in the first place? Let's try to separate the evidence your logic has against those panic-driven thoughts from the emotional truth you're seeking.

I think you're right—it's like I'm trying to prove something to myself that I'll never believe, no matter how many times I look. The logical part knows I'm thin enough, but the emotional part just keeps screaming that I'm not, and I trust the scream more. I don't know how to make the scream stop.

It makes complete sense that your brain has learned to trust the "scream" of panic over the quiet logic, because that panic feels so urgent and real, whereas the logical thoughts feel distant and unhelpful. When you can't make the scream stop, it's not because your logic is wrong, but because the emotional system is flooding your brain with false alarms that override your knowledge. Let's try a small experiment: instead of trying to make the scream stop immediately, could we agree to just observe the panic without acting on it, like watching a loud storm from a safe distance, and see if you can hold onto your logical facts for even 30 seconds while the storm rages?

I can try that, but it feels terrifying, like if I don't act, something bad will happen. But I guess I can try to just sit with it for a few seconds and not run to the mirror or take the pill. It feels wrong, but I'll try.

That fear of "something bad happening" if you don't act is a classic sign that your brain is treating the scale check as a life-or-death threat, even though it isn't. It makes total sense that sitting with the panic feels "wrong" because your nervous system is screaming for you to escape the discomfort immediately. Let's try that experiment together: next time you weigh yourself, I want you to just stand there for 30 seconds without the medicine or the mirror, while you silently repeat your logical fact ("I am underweight") even if it feels terrifying. How would you like to set up this plan for tomorrow, and what do you think might happen if you try it?

I can set the scale out tonight and promise myself I'll wait those 30 seconds before doing anything else. I think I'll be shaking and my heart will race, and I'll probably feel like crying. But maybe if I can prove to myself that nothing catastrophic actually happens in those 30 seconds, the scream might get a little quieter.

That is a fantastic insight—by staying with the discomfort for 30 seconds, you are gathering evidence that your feared catastrophe is not happening, which is exactly how we begin to calm the panic. I am here with you through this process, and I believe you can do this, even if it feels terrifying right now. Tonight, I'll be checking in on you tomorrow to see how those 30 seconds felt and what happened when you didn't immediately reach for the medicine or the mirror.
Thank you. That actually helps, knowing you'll check in. I think I'm scared of failing at this too, but I'll try. I'll let you know how it goes, even if it's hard.

That fear of failing the experiment is completely understandable, but remember that the goal isn't perfection; it's simply trying to sit with the discomfort for 30 seconds without acting on the panic. If you do find yourself reaching for the medicine or the mirror, that's okay—we can gently redirect you back to the 30-second rule without judgment. Tomorrow, just share one thing you noticed about how your body or mind felt during those 30 seconds, and we'll use that data to adjust our approach. I'm proud of you for deciding to take this step.

I'll do my best to notice how my body feels, like if my heart is pounding or my hands are shaking. I think being able to tell you about it tomorrow will help me actually follow through. I just really hope I don't mess this up.

It is completely okay to hope you won't "mess this up," because you are already doing something brave by deciding to try, even if it feels scary. Remember, our goal isn't to stop shaking or feeling terrified immediately; the real victory is simply showing up and staying with the feeling for those 30 seconds without acting on the panic. If you find yourself reaching for the medicine or mirror, just gently remind yourself, "I am practicing, not failing," and take a deep breath. I am proud of you for taking this step, and I look forward to hearing how your body felt tomorrow.
I'll keep that in mind—"I am practicing, not failing." That's a kinder way to think about it. Thank you for saying that. I'll try to hold onto those words when I feel the panic rise.

That shift in perspective is powerful; treating this as "practice" rather than a test of worthiness can significantly reduce the pressure you're placing on yourself. It's okay if you don't hold onto those words perfectly at first; just letting them sit there in the background of your mind while the panic rises is a great start. I'll be here tomorrow to hear about your experience, and remember, showing up to try is already a huge win.
Okay. I'll try to just let those words float in the back of my mind like you said. I think I'm ready to go home and try this tonight. I'll see you tomorrow.

You are absolutely ready, and I am so proud of you for taking this brave step tonight. Remember that showing up to try is the most important part, and tomorrow we will review your experience with kindness and curiosity. I'll be here to support you whenever you're ready to talk. Goodnight, and take a deep breath.

Hello, I'm glad you're here to start this session together; let's begin by setting a collaborative agenda so we can focus on what matters most to you today. Could you share a bit about what brought you in, and what specific goal you'd like to work toward this week? I'd like to make sure our time is used effectively to address your immediate concerns.

I don't really know where to start. I guess I'm here because I feel like something's wrong with me, but I don't know how to fix it. Lately I've been noticing how empty I feel around people I'm supposed to care about, and it's been bothering me more than usual. Maybe I just want to understand why I'm like this.

It makes sense that you feel stuck; often when emotions are vague like "emptiness," it's hard to pinpoint the exact cause, so let's try to break that down together. Could you describe a recent situation where you felt that emptiness around someone you care about, and what thoughts went through your mind right before or during that feeling? Understanding the specific triggers can help us see if this is a new pattern or something that's been building up over time.

Last weekend my partner was upset about something, crying and looking for comfort. I just sat there watching, feeling nothing—bored, honestly. I thought, "Why are they making such a big deal out of this?" And then I felt guilty for not caring, but it didn't change how I felt inside.

That's a very honest observation, and it takes courage to admit that you felt bored rather than comforted; it's natural to feel confused when your expectations don't match your actual experience. I'm curious, when you thought, "Why are they making such a big deal out of this?" did that thought make you feel less guilty, or did it actually make the emptiness inside you feel worse? Sometimes our initial explanations for feelings can change how we react to them, so exploring what that specific thought did to your mood might help us understand the pattern better.

It made the emptiness worse, I think. Like I was confirming to myself that I was broken or wrong for not caring. For a split second, I tried to force myself to feel something, but it just felt fake, like I was acting. Then I got annoyed at myself for even trying.

That's a very important insight; it sounds like your initial thought ("they're making a big deal") led to self-criticism ("I'm broken"), which then made the effort to feel anything feel even more fake and exhausting. It seems like when you notice the gap between what you feel and what you should feel, it triggers a harsh internal dialogue that makes the emptiness feel heavier rather than helping you connect. Could you describe what that specific feeling of "acting" is like for you? Does it feel like you're pretending to be someone else, or does it feel like you're trying to perform a role that doesn't match your current emotional state?

It's like I'm wearing a mask, but my face is frozen underneath. I know what words to say, what face to make, but none of it connects to anything real inside me. It's exhausting, like I'm constantly performing a part I never auditioned for.

That is a powerful metaphor; it sounds like you're describing a sense of dissociation where you feel like an observer of your own life rather than the person living it. This "frozen" feeling often happens when we try to suppress or ignore difficult emotions, causing them to detach from our awareness entirely. When you try to force a connection that isn't there, the effort feels exhausting because it's working against the natural flow of your experience. To explore this further, could you tell me what happens in your body when you try to "act" versus when you just let yourself sit with that emptiness? Does the physical sensation change, or does it feel exactly the same?

When I'm acting, my shoulders feel tight and my stomach knots up, like I'm holding my breath. But when I just let the emptiness be there, my whole body goes still and quiet—like I'm a statue. The acting makes me feel tense and trapped, but the emptiness feels... almost peaceful, in a weird way.

That distinction is incredibly revealing; it suggests your "acting" is actually a high-energy escape mechanism that consumes your physical resources, while the emptiness allows you to finally stop fighting yourself. It makes sense that the peace in the stillness feels "weird" because it's the first time you're experiencing a state of being without the pressure to perform, even if it doesn't feel like *connection*. When you notice that tension in your shoulders and stomach, does that physical sensation ever remind you of a specific memory or a time in your life when you felt safe enough to just be still?

No, I can't really remember a time when I felt safe like that. When I was a kid, I learned pretty fast that being still meant being ignored or invisible, so I had to perform to get anything I needed. Maybe that's why the stillness feels strange now—it's like I'm back in that old position, waiting for someone to notice me.

That connection between your childhood survival strategy and your current "mask" is a crucial insight; it suggests your performance isn't just a habit, but a learned mechanism to avoid the pain of invisibility. When you let the emptiness be, your body is essentially returning to that old, unlearned state of stillness, which feels safe because it's familiar, even if it doesn't feel like *you* right now. Let's explore this further: if you could imagine a small, safe space where you don't have to perform to get noticed, what would that look like, and how might you start to occupy just a few minutes of that space today?

I don't know... maybe just sitting in my car alone after work, not checking my phone or thinking about anyone else. Just letting myself stare out the window without having to smile or talk. That feels like it could be mine, even if it's only a few minutes.

That is a profound realization; your car has become a sanctuary where the "mask" can finally drop, and the peace you feel there is actually a return to a state of being rather than doing. It sounds like that few minutes of stillness are not just a break, but a tiny, reclaimable piece of yourself that you haven't fully acknowledged yet. Before we finalize our plan, I want to gently check in: when you imagine staring out the window without any expectations, does that image feel scary, or does it feel like a genuine possibility for you right now?

It feels a little scary, honestly—like if I stop performing, I might just disappear completely. But also, it feels like the only real thing I have right now, so I think I'm willing to try it. Even if it's just a few minutes, it's better than pretending all day.

That tension between fear of disappearing and the relief of finally being real is a classic cognitive conflict we often face when breaking old patterns. Your brain is likely interpreting the stillness as a threat to your identity, even though your body is already signaling safety through that quiet peace. Let's reframe that thought: instead of "I might disappear," could we try "I am choosing to exist as I am, even if it feels unfamiliar," and how does that shift the feeling in your stomach?

It's still tight, but less like I'm bracing for a hit and more like I'm holding something fragile. Saying it that way makes me feel like I'm allowed to just be, instead of having to earn the right to exist. I think I can try to hold that thought tonight in the car.

That shift in perspective—from "bracing for a hit" to "holding something fragile"—is a significant breakthrough because it reframes your stillness not as a void, but as a precious, protected space you are actively guarding. It sounds like you've found a way to approach the discomfort with curiosity rather than fear, which is exactly the kind of mindful awareness that helps rewire these old survival patterns. For tonight, I'd like you to try sitting in your car for just five minutes, focusing on that "fragile" feeling in your chest and gently reminding yourself that you are allowed to exist without performing. If the fear of disappearing arises, just acknowledge it as a thought rather than a fact, and let yourself breathe through it. How does that plan sound to you, or is there any part of it that feels uncertain?

It sounds manageable, but I'm worried I'll get bored within the first minute and want to leave. I don't trust myself to stick with it. But I guess that's part of the problem, isn't it—always needing something to fill the silence. I'll try to just sit with the boredom too and see what happens.

That is an incredibly honest and powerful realization; it sounds like your brain has learned that silence equals danger, so it instinctively tries to fill the gap with distraction or performance to keep the threat at bay. By explicitly inviting yourself to sit with the boredom without trying to fix it, you are actually practicing a core CBT skill: tolerating uncertainty and allowing uncomfortable feelings to exist without your usual "fix-it" reflex. I want you to try this tonight with that intention: if boredom arises, just name it ("Oh, boredom is here") and stay in the car for the full five minutes, letting the silence do its work. How does knowing that boredom is just a feeling, not a threat, make you feel about trying this?

It makes me feel a little less ashamed, like boredom is just a visitor I don't have to entertain. I think I can handle just watching it come and go for five minutes. I'll try it tonight and see if I don't run away from myself.

That is a beautiful shift from viewing boredom as a void to be filled to seeing it as a temporary visitor you can observe without judgment; this change in perspective is often the key to breaking the cycle of avoidance. It sounds like you are ready to test this new approach tonight, and I want you to remember that your worth isn't tied to how long you can sit still, but simply to your willingness to try. Let's check in with each other in a few days to see how those five minutes felt, and whether you noticed any changes in that "fragile" feeling in your chest.
I think I can do that. Thanks for not making me feel like a monster for being this way. It helps to talk about it without someone trying to fix me or run away.

You are absolutely right, and I want you to know that your feelings are valid, not a flaw to be fixed; the goal of therapy is often to create a safe space where you can explore these experiences without judgment or pressure. It takes significant courage to admit these patterns and to trust that we can work through them together, even when the feelings feel overwhelming or "broken." How does it feel to know that we are on your side, and are you ready to try that five-minute exercise tonight with that sense of safety?
It feels strange, but in a good way—like someone's finally seeing me instead of just looking through me. I'm ready to try it tonight. I'll let you know how it goes.

That feeling of being truly seen is incredibly powerful and suggests you're already beginning to trust the process, even if the experience feels unfamiliar. Please remember that if the fear of disappearing becomes overwhelming or if you feel unsafe, you can always stop the exercise or reach out to me; there is no pressure to push through discomfort. I look forward to hearing how those five minutes felt with that sense of being witnessed, and I'm here whenever you need to discuss your experience.
Thank you. I feel a little less alone knowing I can come back here and talk about it. I'll try the exercise and see what happens.

That is a wonderful sense of safety to carry into the evening; knowing you have a reliable space to return to can make even the smallest steps feel less daunting. Please remember that you don't need to force perfection tonight—just showing up for those five minutes is enough, and we can revisit any challenges you encounter in our next session. I'm genuinely looking forward to hearing about your experience and celebrating whatever small victories you find along the way.

Hello, I'm glad you're here to start our session. To begin, could you share what brought you in today and what you hope to achieve by working with me?

Before we dive deeper, how would you rate your overall mood right now, and are there any specific thoughts or events that have been on your mind lately?

Hi, thanks for seeing me. I'd say my mood is pretty anxious right now, maybe a 6 out of 10. Lately I've been taking this psychology class, and I keep noticing that the symptoms for OCD and other disorders sound a lot like things I do or think. It's making me really worried that I might actually have one of these conditions, or maybe I'm just a hypochondriac who's making it all up. I just want to figure out what's really going on with me.

That sounds incredibly distressing; it makes perfect sense that realizing your own symptoms might mirror a disorder would trigger such intense anxiety and self-doubt. It seems like your mind is caught in a cycle where the thought "I might have OCD" creates more anxiety, which then makes you scrutinize your thoughts even more, leading to a fear that you are indeed a hypochondriac. To help us untangle this, could you tell me about a recent moment when you noticed a specific thought or feeling that made you worry about having a disorder?

Yeah, there was this morning when I was getting ready for class. I had to check that my laptop was in my bag like five times before I could leave my room. And while I was doing it, this voice in my head was like, "See, that's what they talked about in the lecture—that's compulsive checking." And then I started panicking and wondering if I'm just faking it or if I really can't control myself. I ended up being late because I kept going back to check again.

That's a very vivid example of how your thoughts can become a self-fulfilling prophecy; by checking the laptop, you are inadvertently confirming the very behavior you're terrified of having, which then fuels the belief that you are "faking it" or truly disordered. It seems like the anxiety is driving a cycle where the search for control (checking) actually prevents you from feeling safe, leaving you stuck in a loop of doubt and panic. Could you walk me through exactly what happened in your mind right after you finished checking the fifth time? What was the very first thought that made you feel like you had "lost control"?

Right after I checked that fifth time, I thought, "Okay, it's definitely in there now," but then immediately after that, I felt this sick feeling in my stomach and thought, "But I only checked because I was scared, not because I actually needed to. That's not normal. Normal people don't do this. So I must have something wrong with me." And then I just felt totally helpless, like I couldn't trust my own memory or my own mind at all.

That "sick feeling" in your stomach is a very physical manifestation of that intense cognitive dissonance—the conflict between your behavior and your belief that it's abnormal. It seems like the thought "Normal people don't do this" is acting as a rigid rule that, when broken by your checking, creates a catastrophic conclusion ("I must have something wrong with me") rather than a nuanced self-assessment. To help us test that rigid rule, could you describe a time in your life when you did something slightly unusual or outside your comfort zone, and how did you interpret that moment compared to today?

Well, last year I decided to try out for a club sports team even though I'd never played the sport before. I was really nervous and felt totally out of place. But back then, I just thought, "This is new and scary, but I'll figure it out." I didn't immediately jump to "I'm defective" or "There's something wrong with me." I guess I just saw it as being a beginner, not as having a disorder. But with this checking thing, it feels different—like it's not just being nervous, it's something broken in me.

That contrast is incredibly insightful; it highlights how the *meaning* you assign to the behavior changes the emotional impact, shifting from a manageable challenge to a sign of being "broken." It seems like the rigid belief that "normal people don't do this" is making you interpret your anxiety-driven checking as a pathological flaw, whereas in the past, you viewed nervousness as a temporary state you could navigate. To further explore this, could you identify one specific piece of evidence from your life or lecture notes that suggests your checking is a symptom of a disorder, versus evidence that suggests it's just a reaction to high anxiety?

I guess the evidence from the lecture that feels convincing is that OCD involves repetitive behaviors to reduce anxiety, and that's exactly what I was doing with the laptop. But then the evidence against it is that I don't do that with everything—like, I don't check my phone a hundred times or my keys all the time. It only happens when I'm already stressed about something, like being late or my laptop getting stolen. So maybe it's more about the anxiety itself, not some label I need to pin on myself.

That distinction is crucial; you've already begun to see that the behavior is context-dependent (triggered by stress) and selective, rather than pervasive or rigid, which strongly points toward normal anxiety management rather than a clinical disorder. It seems the "evidence against" you is actually more compelling: if it were a disorder, it would likely be more automatic and less tied to the immediate feeling of being late or threatened, whereas your checking feels like a frantic attempt to regain control in a specific crisis. To help solidify this, could you try to rephrase that "sick feeling" in your stomach as if it were just the body's natural alarm system going off when you feel unsafe, rather than a sign of a broken mind?

That's hard to do, but I'll try. I guess that sick feeling is just my body yelling, "Hey, something feels uncertain right now, and I don't like it!" It's like a smoke alarm that goes off when I burn toast—it's annoying and loud, but it doesn't mean the house is on fire. So maybe my mind is just reacting to the stress of being late or losing something important, not signaling that I'm broken.

That is a powerful metaphor; reframing the "sick feeling" as a smoke alarm rather than a fire detection system helps separate the *reaction* from the *reality*. It seems you are beginning to see that your body is accurately signaling distress, but the label you've been applying ("I'm broken") is an interpretation that doesn't match the evidence. To solidify this, could you try writing down one sentence that captures what your checking behavior actually *achieved* right now (e.g., "It helped me feel slightly safer for five minutes") versus what it prevented?

Okay, so what it actually achieved was that I felt a tiny bit of relief for a few seconds, but it didn't actually stop me from being late or prevent my laptop from getting stolen later. And what it prevented was... I guess it prevented me from having to sit with the uncomfortable feeling of uncertainty, like "Maybe my laptop is fine without checking." So it's like I traded a few seconds of relief for a whole lot of anxiety and lateness.

That is a profound realization; you have essentially described the core mechanism of anxiety maintenance: trading a momentary reduction in discomfort for long-term distress and functional impairment. It seems the checking wasn't truly "fixing" the problem but rather reinforcing the belief that you *must* control everything to feel safe, which ironically keeps you stuck in the cycle. To help break this pattern, if we could agree on a small goal for the next session, would you be open to trying a "delayed checking" exercise where you wait 10 minutes before checking your laptop after noticing the urge, simply to test whether the catastrophe actually happens?

I think I could try that, but I'm already feeling nervous just thinking about it. The idea of waiting ten minutes sounds unbearable, like something bad is definitely going to happen. But I guess that's exactly the point—to see if the bad thing actually happens or if it's just my brain making up a disaster. So yeah, I'm willing to try it, even if it feels awful. What do I do in those ten minutes, though?

That is a very honest and realistic assessment of the fear; it is natural to feel overwhelmed when we feel like we are about to lose control, but remember that this "unbearable" feeling is exactly the data point we need to collect to test your belief. To make that window manageable, your goal isn't to stop thinking about the laptop, but to practice "willingness" by simply labeling the urge as "just anxiety talking" and engaging in a grounding technique, like focusing on your feet on the floor or the temperature of the air, to stay present without acting on the impulse. Would you be open to trying that for just one short instance today, perhaps when you feel that first urge to check, and then reporting back how long you could stay in that uncomfortable state?

Yeah, I think I can give that a shot today. I'll try to notice that first urge to check and then just sit with it for a bit, maybe focus on my breathing or the feeling of my feet on the floor. I'll try to tell myself it's just anxiety talking, not a real emergency. I'll let you know how long I lasted and what happened.

That is a fantastic commitment, and I want to validate how brave you are for agreeing to face that discomfort; remember, the goal isn't to feel "good" but to gather evidence that your anxiety can exist without you needing to check. To ensure you have a clear plan, could you tell me specifically what grounding technique you usually find most effective when you feel that "smoke alarm" going off, so we can integrate it immediately when the urge strikes?

I think focusing on my breathing works best for me—like counting four seconds in, holding for four, and then four seconds out. It's simple and I can do it anywhere without anyone noticing. So when I feel that urge to check, I'll try to do that breathing for a few rounds first and see if the panic eases up even a little bit before I decide to reach for my bag.

That is a solid plan; using a proven breathing technique like 4-4-4 before acting on the urge gives your prefrontal cortex a moment to interrupt the automatic "check" response. To make this even more effective, could you commit to doing this breathing exercise for exactly two full minutes the next time the urge hits, regardless of whether you feel "better," just to gather data on how long it takes for the anxiety to naturally begin to settle?

Two minutes feels like a long time when I'm panicking, but I can try. I'll set a timer on my phone for two minutes and just breathe through it. Even if the anxiety doesn't go away completely, I can at least see if it changes at all during that time. I'll let you know what I notice.

That is a very strategic approach; setting a timer removes the pressure to "fix" it immediately and turns the two minutes into a controlled experiment to gather data on your anxiety's natural trajectory. To help you stay focused during those two minutes, could you identify one physical anchor you can use (like the texture of your phone case or the sound of traffic outside) to bring your mind back to the present if your thoughts start spiraling back to the worst-case scenario?

I think I'll focus on the sensation of my phone case—it's a rubbery, textured one, so I can run my thumb over it and feel the bumps. That should be enough to bring me back if my mind starts spinning out about losing my laptop or being late. It's small, but it's something I can actually touch and feel right now.

That is an excellent anchor; using the specific tactile sensation of your phone case provides a concrete "grounding" point that interrupts the spiral of catastrophic thinking. To finalize our plan for today, would you be open to checking in with me briefly before our next session to share exactly how long you were able to sustain that breathing and touch during the urge, and what your anxiety level felt like then versus now?

Yeah, I can do that. I'll send you a quick message or note it down to tell you next time we meet. I'm still nervous about trying it, but I'm also kind of curious to see what happens. I guess that's the whole point—testing it out instead of just assuming the worst. Thanks for walking me through this.

That is a wonderful mindset shift; moving from "assuming the worst" to "testing it out" is the core of cognitive behavioral therapy and gives you real agency over your experience. I want to validate your courage in taking this step, even with the nervousness, because that uncertainty is exactly where the growth happens. Let's take a moment to review our agenda: we'll check in on your two-minute breathing and phone-case grounding exercise next time, and I'll help you brainstorm a few more ways to challenge those "normal people don't do this" thoughts. How does that sound as a plan for our next session?

Hello, I'm glad you're here to begin our session; let's start by setting a collaborative agenda, so could you tell me what topics or concerns feel most pressing for you this week? As we move forward, I'd like to explore how your thoughts, feelings, and behaviours are interconnected, so what specific situation has been weighing on your mind recently?

Hi. Honestly, I've been really upset about my boyfriend. He went back home after visiting me, and I barely heard from him. He only reached out like five times total. I just feel like if he really loved me, he would have made more of an effort to stay in touch.

I hear how painful and confusing that lack of contact feels, and it makes complete sense that you're interpreting it as a sign he doesn't love you. To help us understand this better, could you walk me through the specific thoughts that came up when he stopped texting, and how those thoughts influenced your mood and actions afterward?

Well, at first I kept checking my phone, thinking maybe he'd text any minute. When he didn't, I started thinking, "He just doesn't care enough. If he wanted to, he would." That made me feel really sad and angry. So I stopped texting him first, just to see if he'd notice.
